title: Welcome
text: This guide explains how to use your company's operations platform: the one place for work orders, purchasing, quality, safety, people matters, books and reports. It is written for the people who use it every day, not for programmers. Where something is only for the person who sets the system up, you will see a short box that points to the Administrator brief. What the system is Think of it as your company's intranet with the work built in. When you sign in you land on Home : company news, the things waiting for you, and quick links. The menu on the left leads to the areas of the business you are allowed to use. Each area keeps its own records (a work order, a purchase order, a nonconformance, an expense report), and records that need a decision go to the right person as an approval. A few ideas run through everything: You see what your job needs. The menu, the pages and the buttons depend on your role and on the sites you work at. See Roles and access . Nothing is lost half-way. Forms keep what you typed while you work, and the technician screens keep working without a connection. See Getting started and Working offline and on tablets . Decisions leave a trail. Approvals, sign-offs and changes are recorded with who did them and when. The system tells you what is late. Notifications, reminders and the What is late page pull overdue work into one place. Where things are in this guide The groups below match the groups in the left-hand menu of the application. Getting started Sign in, find your way around, save your work. How I like to work Text size, spacing, contrast and more. News, people, policies Announcements, the directory and the handbook. Improvements Suggest an idea and follow it to measured savings. Maintenance Assets, work orders, preventive maintenance, storerooms. Field service Agreements, dispatch and the technician's day. Production Production orders, planning, shop floor and shift log. Quality and safety Quality, CAPA, documents, safety, changes, continuity. Sales and supply Customers, quotes, purchasing, leasing. Finance Books, budgets, receivables and payables. Insight Reports and the what-is-late view. Administrator brief Setting the system up for your company. Glossary Plain-language meanings of the terms used here. Numbered steps describe a task from start to finish. Who can do this boxes name the role that holds the right. If you do not have it, the button or page will not appear, or the system will say you may not. Administrator boxes are short notes for the person who configures the system, with a link to the full steps. Use the search box at the top of the guide to find a word, such as “timesheet” or “supplier”. The print view gives you a clean copy of any page. Your menu may not show every area described in this guide. That is normal: your company chooses which parts to switch on, and your role decides the rest. Why some menu items are missing explains how to tell which reason applies.

title: Getting started
text: This page takes you from the sign-in screen to a confident first day: how to get in, what the menu is telling you, where to look for what needs your attention, and how the system protects the things you type. Signing in Most companies use single sign-on : you sign in with the same company account you use for email, so there is no separate password for this system. Open the address your company gave you. The page is titled Sign in . Type your work email in Work email . Choose Continue with your company account . You go to your company's own sign-in page; sign in there as usual. You come back to the platform and land on Home . If you opened a link to a particular page before signing in, you are taken to that page instead. If the page says your company or email is not set up, or that you are not a user, ask your administrator. Signing in does not create an account; someone has to add you first. Signing in with an issued token Below the button there is a fold-out called Development sign-in with an API token . A token is a long code, beginning erp_ , that stands in for a password. Your administrator may hand one out for trials and demonstrations, or for a device that cannot use company sign-in. Paste it into API token and choose Sign in with token . Each token signs you in as one specific person, so never share yours. Tokens can be switched off for the company once single sign-on works, and single sign-on is set up per company. See Administrator brief: sign-in . If you see “Your session has ended. Sign in again.”, the system no longer recognises your sign-in. This is normal after you sign out in another window, or after your sign-in expires. Sign in again; anything you had typed into a form is waiting for you (see Saving and autosaved drafts ). The menu on the left The left-hand menu is grouped by area. On a phone or a narrow window it hides behind the Menu button at the top; press Esc or choose Close menu to put it away again. The counts refresh each time you move to another page. Why some menu items are missing If a page described in this guide is not in your menu, one of four things is true. They are checked in this order: Your company has hidden it from your role. Companies can switch features on or off for each role. A hidden feature leaves the menu, and if you open its address directly you see Not available : “This part of the platform is turned off for your role.” An administrator can turn it on under Admin → Features . Your edition does not include it. The Lite edition covers the intranet, policies, expenses, customers and invoicing, suppliers and bills, the built-in books, data import and their reports. Maintenance, production, quality, safety and the rest are Standard. In Lite the menu shows only those areas, and the top-left name reads “Intranet · Lite”. See not licensed . Your role does not allow it. Each page needs a permission. For example Books needs the right to see the books, and Time shows if you are linked to an employee record or you approve or export time. See Roles and access . It is not licensed for your site. Field service appears only where field service has been licensed. You do not need to know which reason applies. Ask your administrator, and say which menu entry you expected. They can see your roles and your features. Home Home is the first page after sign-in: company news, a My work list of what is waiting for you, upcoming events and quick links. Home and approvals explains each block. Search The search box at the top of every page looks across people, policies, announcements and, where you have access, assets, documents, work orders, customers and suppliers. Click the box that says Search people, policies, assets… and type at least two characters. Press Enter . Results appear grouped by kind: People , Policies , Announcements , Assets , Documents , Work orders , Customers , Suppliers . Click a result to open it. Search shows you only what you may open. If “Nothing found” appears for something you know exists, it may be at a site you have no access to, or in a feature that is hidden from your role. On Home there is a separate box, Find a colleague , that goes straight to the people directory. The notifications bell The bell in the top bar shows how many unread notifications you have. Click it to open Notifications . See Notifications and reminders . Approvals When something needs your sign-off (an expense report, a purchase request, a document, a change), it appears under My day → Approvals and on Home. See Home and approvals . Saving and autosaved drafts You rarely need to worry about losing a half-finished form. About one second after you stop typing, the system saves what you entered on the form as a draft , on the server, under your name. title: Roles and access
text: What you can see and do in the platform is decided by your roles and by the sites where you hold them. This page explains both in plain terms, describes the roles most companies start with, and helps you read the messages you get when something is off limits. How access works A permission is one small right, such as “see work orders” or “approve timesheets”. A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as Maintenance Technician or Buyer / Purchasing. An administrator assigns roles to people. Each assignment is either company-wide or limited to one site (or a named group of sites). If you hold several roles, you have everything they give you together. The menu, the tabs on a page and the buttons all follow your permissions. A button you cannot use is usually not shown at all. The full list of permissions and which page each opens is on the Permissions table . Sites and facilities A site (the system also says “facility”) is a plant, store, building or office. Your role assignment says where it applies: Company-wide: you can use the permission at every site. People in head office roles usually have this. One site, or a group of sites: you can use the permission at those sites only. A district manager may hold a role across a group; a store manager at a single store. Site limits are enforced by the database itself, not only by the screens. If a record belongs to a site you have no role at, it will not show up in lists or in search, and opening it directly is refused. You can hold different roles at different sites; for example, technician at one plant and maintenance manager at another. Administrators assign roles and sites under Admin → People and access . See Administrator brief: sites and people . The starter roles Every company starts with the roles below. They cannot be edited, but an administrator can add company roles of their own (a named set of permissions), so your company's list may be longer. Everyone, whatever their role, can also suggest improvements, claim expenses and read published policies. Role In plain words Administrator Everything, including setup: sites, people, sign-in, features, retention, archives and imports. Maintenance Manager Runs maintenance: assets, work orders, parts and storerooms, documents, training and qualifications; approves timesheets; sees reports. Operations / Plant Manager Runs a plant: production, planning, quality and safety views, continuity, site visits, sales orders; approves timesheets; posts announcements. Production Supervisor / Planner Plans and runs production orders, shop-floor work, planning and imports; requests purchases. Operator / Requester Raises work requests, reports quality and safety problems, runs operations on the shop floor. Maintenance Technician Carries out work orders, records labor and parts, raises requests, reports quality and safety issues; sees assets, documents and stock. Field Technician Works their own service visits from a tablet: reports and customer sign-off. Service Dispatcher Plans and assigns field service visits, agreements, technicians and vehicles; prepares quotes. Quality Reviewer / Quality Manager Contains and dispositions nonconformances, owns and verifies corrective actions; the manager also controls documents. EHS / Safety Reviewer Investigates and classifies safety incidents; works on continuity plans. Trainer / Evaluator Assigns training, records attendance and shadowing, signs practical evaluations, sees training records. Property / Facilities Manager Maintenance for buildings and leased units: work orders, leasing, rent billing, site visits. District / Area Manager Oversees several sites: work requests and verification, safety, site visits and reports. Store / Site Manager Day-to-day at one site: raises requests, verifies finished work, reports problems, sees site visits. Buyer / Purchasing Suppliers and prices, purchase orders, receiving, parts catalog; sees payables. Finance Approver Approves supplier invoices, releases credit holds, reviews larger expenses, manages budgets and business cases. Accounts Payable Clerk Captures and processes supplier invoices. Billing / Accounts Receivable Invoices shipments, records payments, works the collections queue. Bookkeeper Keeps the built-in books, bank review and period lock; payables and receivables; expenses; accounting connection. Sales Representative / Sales Manager Customers, opportunities and quotes; the manager also turns quotes into orders. Payroll Administrator Sees every timesheet and produces the payroll export. HR Manager Employee records, training assignment and records, performance reviews, policies and announcements. Executive (read-only, consolidated) Reads across the company, including reports, books and business cases; changes nothing. Two things are not roles. Approving an expense report or a purchase request depends on being named in the approval route (a role at the site, a department head, or someone covering for them), not on a separate permission. And performance reviews are open to the employee and their reviewer without any permission; HR sees all. Why you may be told “no” When an action is refused, the message says why. title: Working offline and on tablets
text: Plants, basements and rural sites often have poor wifi. The platform is built so that a technician's day does not stop when the connection does. This page explains what keeps working offline, what does not, how to use the outbox, and how to put the app on a tablet or phone. What works offline Offline support covers the maintenance technician's core routine on work orders and the field technician's day on My day . Two things make it work: Saved copies. While you are online, the app keeps a copy on your device of your My work orders list and of each work order you open. When the connection drops, you still see those, marked “Copy saved on this device [time]: no connection right now.” The outbox. Three kinds of change can be made without a connection: labor hours, parts used , and status changes ( Start work , Put on hold , Mark complete ). Each is kept on the device, in the order you made it, until it can be sent. On My day the changes are starting a visit , saving the service report draft and submitting the service report (labor, parts, notes, readings, recommended repairs and the customer's signature). You can do offline You need a connection for Open a work order you have looked at before, or one on your saved list Work orders you have never opened on this device Record labor on it Creating a new work order Record a part used Looking up stock levels or parts Start, hold or complete the work Opening documents and procedures (the viewer needs a connection) See today's visits and each visit's details on My day; start a visit; fill in, save and submit the service report with labor, parts and signature A day or a visit you have never opened on this device; the office's view of the report and billing Everything outside work orders and My day, such as approvals, expenses, timesheets and reports Offline use is specific to work orders and My day . Do not rely on it for other screens. Open My day (and the work orders you need) once with a connection before you go where the signal is weak: that is when the copies are saved. My day offline Open Field service → My day while you are online. The tablet saves the day, each visit's details and report draft, and the parts list. With no connection the page shows Offline and Copy saved on this device . Tap Start the visit , fill in the report and tap Submit report . The stop shows Waiting to send , and each queued change is listed under it ( Start the visit , Service report draft , Submit the service report ). When the connection returns the changes are sent in order. A repeat of a change that already went through is recognised by its key and not applied twice. A change the server refuses stays on the stop, and on Changes made offline , as Refused with the reason. Correct the report reopens the form with your entries; Discard drops it. See Field service: My day for what each step does. The connection bar A bar appears under the top bar whenever the state is not normal: The bar says Meaning Offline: showing copies saved on this device. N changes will be sent when you are back online. No connection. You are looking at saved copies; anything you record is waiting in the outbox. Sending N changes made offline… The connection is back and the outbox is being sent. N changes waiting to be sent. Send now You are online, but some changes have not gone yet. Choose Send now to try immediately. … N changes could not be saved. Review The server refused one or more. They stay in the outbox with the reason. No bar means you are online and nothing is waiting. Using the outbox The page Changes made offline (opened from Review in the bar, or from see all on a work order) lists everything waiting on this device. Work normally while offline. Each labor entry, part or status change you record is added to the outbox, and the work order shows “Waiting to be sent” with what is queued. When you are back online, the app sends the outbox automatically: as soon as the connection returns, and again every minute. You can also choose Send now . Open Changes made offline to check. Each row shows when it was made, what it is (for example “1.5 h labor on 2026-10-23”, “Part used × 2”, “Start work”, “Start the visit”, “Submit the service report”), the work order or my day link, and its state: Waiting or Refused . For a Refused row, read the reason. If you can fix the cause (for example the work order was meanwhile cancelled or completed by someone else, or a rule was not met), choose Try again . If the change is no longer wanted, choose Discard ; you are asked to confirm, and it will not be recorded. The system sends changes in order, and a refusal of one does not stop the rest. A change is never sent twice: each carries a unique key, so if the network drops just as a change goes through, sending it again does not post it a second time. The server applies the same rules as if you had been online, so offline work never skips a check. For example, a status change that is not allowed from the work order's current status is refused with the reason. Before you sign out, make sure the outbox is empty. Signing out removes the saved copies and any unsent changes from the device, and the system warns you first. See Signing out safely . Using a tablet or phone The layout adapts to narrow screens; the menu hides behind the Menu button. Pick a larger text size and a roomier layout under How I like to work if you wear gloves or work at arm's length. Your sign-in belongs to the browser tab. If the tablet is shared, sign out at the end of the shift (after the outbox is empty). The offline copies and the outbox are kept per person on the device, so a colleague who signs in on the same tablet does not see yours. Installing the app You can install the platform as an app, so it opens in its own window from the home screen and starts even with no connection. Installing is optional; the app also works in

title: Home and approvals
text: Home is where each day starts: the company's news, a short list of what needs you, and quick links. Approvals is where you sign off requests that came to you. This page covers both, plus Reviews (records that must be looked at again every so often) and what to do when you are away. Your Home page Home greets you by first name and shows the date. From top to bottom: Find a colleague A search box at the top. Type a name, team or site and press Enter to open the people directory with the search applied. Company news The latest four announcements. Safety notices, events, people news and IT news have their own labels. All news and events opens the full list. Hidden if your company has switched news off for your role. My work A short list of counts, each a link: Waiting for my sign-off , Policies to read and acknowledge , My actions , My open work orders , My training to do and Overdue work orders at my sites . A coloured count means something is overdue or waiting. Items only appear if you have the matching feature and role. Documents to read Controlled documents you must read and acknowledge, with the due date or Overdue . Open each one and acknowledge it on its own page. Unsaved entries Forms you started and did not save; they are kept for you on any device. Click one to continue. See Saving and autosaved drafts . Coming up Events with a date, from the news page. Quick links The employee handbook, the people directory, and links your company added. Links to other websites open in a new tab. Below those blocks, tables list My work orders , Waiting for my sign-off and My training , as far as they apply to you. Click a row to open it. Administrators may also see a card called Worth a look with a suggestion for something to set up. Choose Show me , Not now , or Stop these suggestions . At most one is shown a week; see How I like to work . Approvals An approval is a request that needs one or more people to say yes. Approvals appear under My day → Approvals and on Home. The page title is Waiting for my sign-off . The list contains only steps you can sign right now : earlier stages are finished, you hold the role the step is addressed to (or the step is addressed to you personally, or you are covering for someone), and you are not the person who raised the request. What can arrive Label on the card What you are approving Change review, Startup authorization A change request or its start-up review. See Changes and notices . Purchase request A request to buy. The card shows the total, whether it is capital spend, who asked, and any reason it needed approval. See Purchasing . Quote pricing A quote priced below the company's limits. See Quotes and orders . Document review, Document signature A new document version. A signature asks you to enter your sign-in credential again. See Document control . FMEA review, Continuity plan approval Risk analyses and continuity plans. See Quality and Continuity . Expense reports These appear here too, and you can also decide them on the report itself. See Expenses . Deciding on an approval Open Approvals . Each request is a card. The first line says what it is and which step is yours (for example Finance review ). If you are covering for someone, it says on behalf of their name. Click the title to open the full record and check the details. Some cards link a Justification presentation . Type a comment. It is required to reject , and for some reviews it is required to approve too; then the label reads “Result of your review (required: what you checked and any conditions)”. If the card asks you to sign, enter your sign-in credential in the box provided (at least 8 characters). Choose Approve as [your role] or Reject . The card disappears and the requester is notified. Anyone who holds the role a step is addressed to, at the request's site, can approve it, or a person named personally on the step, or a delegate (below). You can never approve your own request. Separation of duties is deliberate. A very small company may allow the requester to approve their own expense report or bill if nobody else could; the record shows it as self-approved. What the statuses mean Status Meaning Pending The step is open and waiting for a decision. Approved The step was signed. When all stages are approved, the request goes ahead. Rejected A reviewer said no. The requester sees your comment and normally revises and resubmits. Cancelled The requester withdrew the request. Superseded The request was changed and replaced by a newer revision, so earlier approvals no longer count. Away? Delegate your sign-offs At the bottom of the Approvals page, Away? Delegate your sign-offs lets someone else sign for you for a set time. Their signature records that it was on your behalf. Under Delegate to , choose a person. Set From and Until dates. Give a Reason , such as “vacation”. Choose Delegate . The table shows Scheduled before the start date, Active during, and Ended after you press End . Delegating does not give the person your permissions. It only lets them sign the steps addressed to you. A delegate cannot approve your own requests. Reviews My day → Reviews appears for people who manage records that must be looked at again every so often: FMEAs, procedures, policies, course content, suppliers, PM plans, spares lists, control limits, user access and more. It lists what is overdue or due soon. Choose the kind of record, or leave All kinds . Choose Due soon or overdue or All, with their next date . On a row, choose Record review . Choose Still current, no change if the record is still correct, or Changes needed (revise it through its own approval) and say what needs to change (required). Choose Save review . The next review counts from today. If changes are needed, make them on the record itself; they go through that record's normal approval. title: Notifications and reminders
text: Notifications are the system's way of tapping you on the shoulder: something is waiting for you, a request of yours was decided, or something you own is overdue. This page explains where they appear, what creates them, why you may not get the same one twice, and how to turn kinds off. Where you see them The bell in the top bar shows a count of unread notifications. Click it to open the list. My day → Notifications (title For you ) lists them, newest first, up to the latest 50. Email , once a day, if you have unread items and email is switched on for you (see the daily summary ). Using the list Open Notifications . Unread items have a dot beside the headline. Click an item. It is marked read and you go straight to the record it is about (a work order, an approval, a timesheet). To tidy up without opening each one, choose Mark all read . To see only what you have not dealt with, tick Only unread . When the list is empty it says “Nothing here. You are all caught up.” Marking a notification read does not complete the task behind it; the work order is still late, the approval still waits. For that, use Home and approvals . What creates notifications There are two sorts. Events happen at once when something is done to a record that involves you. Reminders are produced by a daily check that looks for things that are due, late or expiring. Most of the common kinds can be muted under Settings on the Notifications page (“Notify me when…”); a few, such as a published policy to read or a performance review notice, are not listed there and always arrive. Events You are told when… Who gets it Something is waiting for your sign-off Whoever holds the role (or their delegate) Your request is approved or rejected The requester A work order or an action is assigned to you The assignee A request comes in through a site's request link Site managers Training is assigned to you The employee Your timesheet is sent back The employee Items you requested arrive; an order from your quote ships; a production order for your sales order is finished The requester or quote owner An order goes on credit hold People who can release credit holds A control chart signals or a measurement is out of tolerance; a nonconformance is raised; an audit is planned or reported Quality people, auditors and auditees A safety incident is reported Safety people at the site A shift log is handed over Supervisors An improvement idea is suggested, owned or decided Leads; the owner; the person who suggested it You own a corrective action, or you are on an 8D team The owner or team member A continuity exercise is scheduled or falls short The facilitator; the plan owner A policy is published The people it applies to (please read and acknowledge) A performance review is opened, shared or ready to acknowledge The employee and the reviewer An expense report is ready to reimburse, or has been reimbursed Finance; the claimant A field service visit or day is assigned The technician You are never notified about something you did yourself. Reminders A daily check creates reminders such as: Your work orders are overdue; PM plans are due with no work order (planners). Your training is due or overdue; your qualifications are expiring. You have not submitted last week's timesheet; timesheets are waiting for your approval. Corrective and safety actions are overdue; corrective-action verifications are due; calibrations are due. Purchase orders are late (buyers); supplier invoices wait for approval; customer invoices are overdue; sales and collections follow-ups are due; a quote you sent expires soon (one notice at 7 days, one at 2 days, and one the day after, not more). Condition readings were missed; leases end without renewal; kits are short of parts for work due soon. A record is due for its periodic review, or a performance review is due or overdue. Your administrator decides which reminders are on, how often they repeat, and who is told. See Administrator brief: reminders and retention . Why you do not get the same one twice Reminders carry a memory. A reminder about the same item for the same person is created once per period (your administrator sets it per reminder: daily, weekly, or just once), not every time the daily check runs. This keeps the bell useful. If a reminder reached you and you have not fixed the cause, the next one comes when the period is up. Opening or reading a notification does not trigger a new one; fixing the cause (submitting the timesheet, completing the work order) stops them. Choosing what you are told about Open Notifications and scroll to Settings . Under Notify me when… , untick the kinds you do not want. The change saves at once. Tick it again to turn it back on. Muting a kind stops new notifications of that kind being created for you; they are not hidden after the fact. Do not mute Something is waiting for my sign-off if you approve things for other people, or you will not know they are waiting. The daily email summary If you tick Email me a daily summary of unread items (on by default), the system builds one email per day with up to 50 of your unread notifications that have not been emailed before, each with a link. It is sent to the email address on your user record, shown beside the checkbox. If you have nothing unread, or you already read everything, no email is sent. Items that were emailed are not included again. The daily summary and the reminder check run in the nightly scheduled job ( Admin → Scheduled jobs ). Email is delivered only when the system has a mail server set up (the Email card on the Scheduled jobs page says whether it has, and Send a test email to me checks it). Until then summaries are prepared but not delivered to inboxes. The delivery code has been tested only against a stand-in mail server, not yet against a real provider, so confirm with the test email before telling people to expect it. title: Time and expenses
text: Two things in My day touch your pay: Time (your weekly timesheet) and Expenses (money you spent for the company and want back). This page covers both: how to fill them in, who approves them, and what each status means. Timesheets A timesheet covers one week, Monday to Sunday. Hours you book to work orders appear on it by themselves. You add everything else (training, meetings, leave) and then submit the week for approval. The My time tab is for anyone linked to an employee record. If your user is not linked to one, the page says so and there is no timesheet for you; ask your administrator. The Team tab is for people who approve time (maintenance managers and plant managers, for instance) or see all timesheets (payroll, HR). Payroll export is for payroll administrators. Fill in and submit your week Open My day → Time . The current week is shown. Use the arrows to go to earlier weeks; you cannot go past the current one. This week brings you back. Check the day boxes and the table. Rows marked from work order are hours you or a colleague recorded on a work order; they are read-only here. To correct them, change the work order. To add other time, pick the Day , the Type (for example Regular hours, Paid time off, Holiday, Sick leave, Unpaid leave), the Hours (in quarter-hours) and an optional note such as “training”. Choose Add time . Use Remove to delete a line you added by mistake. Read any yellow warnings. You are warned when worked hours in the week go over 40, or a single day shows more than 12 hours. The system does not calculate overtime; your approver and your payroll provider handle that. Choose Submit week for approval . The button needs at least some hours on the sheet. Once submitted, the week's work-order hours are locked. If something changes, ask your supervisor to send the sheet back. Timesheet statuses Status Meaning What you can do Not started You have opened no sheet for the week yet. Open it and add time. Draft You are still filling it in. Add or remove time; submit. Waiting for approval Submitted. Hours are locked. Wait; ask your supervisor to send it back if it is wrong. Sent back Your supervisor returned it with a note, shown on the sheet and in Recent weeks . Fix what the note says and submit again. Approved Signed off. Nothing, unless a supervisor reopens it. Sent to payroll Included in a payroll file. The week is locked. Corrections after this are made in payroll. Approving time Open Time → Team . Choose the week (it starts on last week). The summary shows how many are waiting, approved or not submitted. Rows waiting for approval are highlighted. Click a person. Their sheet opens with the same day boxes, table and warnings. Choose Approve [hours] h , or write a note and choose Send back . The note is required to send back and tells the employee what to fix. To change an approved sheet that has not yet gone to payroll, write a reason and choose Reopen . You can never approve your own timesheet. If you entered a sheet on someone else's behalf, someone else must approve it. A sheet already sent to payroll cannot be reopened here. Payroll export Payroll administrators use Time → Payroll export to create a file of approved hours: Choose the From week and To week , and a Layout : one line per person, week and earning code, or per person, day and earning code. Read the preview. Timesheets that are not approved are listed as not ready and stay out of the file; they can go into a later one. Choose Create payroll file , then Download it from Payroll files . Exported weeks are locked. Under Earning codes , set the code your payroll provider expects for each type of hours. Pay rates, overtime, taxes and payments stay in your payroll provider. A reminder tells people who have not submitted last week's timesheet, and tells approvers when sheets are waiting. See Administrator brief: reminders and retention . Approvers are anyone who holds the approve-time permission at the site; see Roles and access . Expenses An expense report is a bundle of expenses (lines) for one trip or purpose, with receipts. You submit it, one or more people approve it, and then finance records the reimbursement. Everyone can claim expenses. All reports is for finance (bookkeepers, finance approvers, accounts payable). Approval rules is for those who manage expenses. Claim an expense Open My day → Expenses . Under New expense report type a title, such as “Customer visit, Chicago”, and the business purpose, then choose Start report . Under Add an expense , set the date, pick the Category , and enter the amount. For Mileage (personal vehicle) enter the miles instead; the system multiplies by the company's rate. Add a merchant and a description. For business meals, also say who attended and why. Choose Add expense . Repeat for each expense. Attach a receipt to each line with Attach (a photo or a PDF, up to 10 MB). Replace swaps it. Read the notes beside each line (see below) and fix or explain them. The banner reads Ready to submit when all is in order. Check the Approval route , then choose Submit for approval . The categories start as: Airfare, Lodging, Meals while traveling, Business meals with guests, Taxi/rideshare/rental car, Mileage, Parking and tolls, Office and shop supplies, Training and conferences, Phone and internet, Tools and small equipment, and Other (explain). Your company may have changed them. Fix and Explain flags Each line is checked against the company's expense rules (see Expense rules ). A flag marked Fix blocks submission; Explain lets you submit if you type an explanation (at least five characters) in the line's Explanation box. Flag Kind What to do The date is in the future; no category; no amount or miles; trip not described; attendees missing; “Other” without a description; mileage rate not set Fix Correct the line. If the mileage rate is not set, finance must set it before mileage can be claimed. Receipt required over the limi

title: Training and performance
text: This page covers two people topics in My day : Training , where you complete courses assigned to you and see which qualifications you hold, and Performance , where you and your manager hold reviews and check-ins and agree goals. Training My day → Training (title Training and qualifications ) has up to three tabs. The first two need you to be linked to an employee record. My training Courses assigned to you, with a status and a due date. Overdue ones are flagged. My qualifications What you are authorized to do, with the date it took effect, when it expires, and a certificate to open as a PDF where one was issued. External credentials (licences, certificates from outside bodies) are listed beneath. Team records Everyone's training and results, for trainers and HR only. Anyone with training access (most roles) sees their own tabs. Team records needs the right to see other people's training records, held by trainers, HR managers and maintenance managers because scores and evidence are sensitive. Assigning training is for trainers, HR and maintenance managers; recording attendance and shadowing is for trainers (instructors); signing practical evaluations is for evaluators. Completing a course does not authorize you to do the work. A qualification is a separate decision granted by an authorized person. Work orders and machines can require a qualification and will refuse a person without a current one. Complete an assigned course A course is a series of numbered steps . Each step has a kind and is completed by a particular person. Kind of step Who completes it Video, Self-study You. Choose I have completed this when you have watched or read it. A linked document opens with Open and its number. Classroom A trainer records attendance ( Record attendance ). On-the-job shadowing A trainer signs it off ( Sign off shadowing ). Practical evaluation An evaluator watches you and signs Competent or Not yet competent with a note about what they observed. You cannot sign your own. Assessment You, by taking the quiz. Open Training → My training and click the course. Work through the steps in order. Each card shows what is done, who recorded it and when. For a step you complete yourself, do the work and choose I have completed this . For steps that need a trainer or evaluator, the card tells you who records it (“A trainer records this for you.”). When every step is done, the course shows Training completed . If the course leads to a qualification, an authorized person still has to grant it. Taking an assessment On the assessment step, choose Take the assessment . Read the pass mark and which attempt this is (“attempt 1 of 3”, for example). Answer each question; where marked, select all answers that apply. Choose Submit answers . You see your score, and whether you passed. If you did not pass and have attempts left, take it again. If you have none left, ask your trainer to re-assign the course. Training statuses Status Meaning Assigned Given to you; nothing recorded yet. In progress At least one step is done. Completed All steps are done. Cancelled Withdrawn; you no longer need to complete it. Overdue A tag next to the due date: not finished by that date. Qualification statuses Status Meaning Active Current. You may do the work it covers. Expired Past its expiry date. Renew before doing covered work. Revoked Withdrawn by an authorized person. Not yet effective Granted with a start date in the future. You are reminded when training is due and when a qualification is about to expire; see Notifications and reminders . Courses, assessments, qualification definitions and certificates are set up by people with course-authoring rights; periodic review of course content shows up under Reviews (see Home and approvals ). Training can be hidden from roles under Admin → Features ; if hidden, qualification checks on work orders and machines still apply. See Administrator brief: features and editions . Performance Performance holds reviews with your manager at the frequency your company sets, check-ins in between, and the goals you agree. Only you, your reviewer and HR can see yours. The menu entry Performance shows if you are linked to an employee record, or if you run the programme in HR. Tab Who sees it What it shows My reviews You Your reviews and check-ins, and your open goals. My team Reviewers Reviews and check-ins you are to complete for the people you review. Everyone HR Every review, with counts of overdue, open and those without a reviewer. Settings HR How the programme runs. Your review A review opens automatically a few weeks before it is due, and you are notified. Your reviewer is normally your manager (set on your employee record), else your department head; HR assigns one if neither exists. Open Performance → My reviews and click your review. The headline tells you what is expected of you: for example “Your reviewer is preparing this. Add your self-assessment below.” If your company asks for one, write your Self-assessment : what went well, what was hard, and what you would like to work on. Choose Submit self-assessment . You can Update self-assessment while the review is open. Your reviewer writes the assessment and goals, then shares the review with you. You are notified: “Your performance review is ready to read and acknowledge”. Read it. Optionally add a comment and choose Acknowledge . Acknowledging says you have read it; it does not mean you agree with all of it. Reviewing someone Open My team and click a review. For a review, choose an Overall rating from your company's scale, and write Strengths , To develop and a Summary . For a check-in, write What was discussed . Add Goals with a measure and a due date. When a goal ends, set its outcome: met, partly met, not met or dropped. Choose Save draft as you go. When ready, choose Share with the employee (for a check-in, Complete check-in ). A rating and a summary are required. Review stat

title: How I like to work
text: People read screens differently. The page My day → How I like to work lets you change how the platform looks for you : how much space there is, how big the text is, how strong the contrast is, and whether reports open as charts or tables. Nobody else's screens change, and your choices follow you to any device you sign in on. This page also explains the fit interview and the occasional “worth a look” suggestion that administrators may see. Your display settings Every setting takes effect the moment you choose it. There is no Save button. Group Choices Good for How much room Roomy: more space between things , Normal , Compact: more on the screen Roomy for touch screens and gloves, compact for big monitors and long tables. Text size Normal , Large , Larger Reading at a distance or with tired eyes. Reports open as Charts first, then the table ; The table first, charts folded away Pick the form you read faster. See Reports . Seeing and moving Stronger contrast ; Reduce motion and animation Bright rooms, low vision, or if movement on screen is distracting or uncomfortable. Open My day → How I like to work . Choose an option in any group. The screens change at once. If you do not like the result, choose the previous option again. If your browser or computer already magnifies text, try Normal here first. Combining both can make pages very large. If the page shows an error in red under the options, the choice could not be saved (for example, you have lost your connection). Your screens may look changed until you reload; choose the option again once you are back online. Worth a look: gentle suggestions Administrators sometimes see a small card on Home called Worth a look . It says what the system noticed in the company's own records (for example, parts being issued often with no reorder level set) and what a feature could do about it. It is never a pop-up, never blocks anything, never shows a price, and appears at most once a week. Show me takes you to the feature. Not now dismisses it; the same suggestion is not shown again for a while. Stop these suggestions opens this page, where administrators have an extra group, Suggestions , with a tick box: “Show me a ‘worth a look’ idea now and then (at most one a week)”. Untick it to stop them for you. Only administrators are shown suggestions, and the suggestions card does not appear in the Lite edition. If you are not an administrator you will not see the group on this page. The company can also switch suggestions off for everyone. They are based only on counts of the company's own records; nothing leaves the system. The fit interview The fit interview is for the person setting the system up, not for everyday users. It lives under Admin → Fit interview , so you will see it in the menu only if you are an administrator. You answer plain questions about the business: what the company makes or does, how many sites and people, whether it keeps stock, buys from suppliers, sends quotes, services customers' equipment, rents space, keeps timesheets and expense claims, needs the system to keep the books, and what customers or regulators require it to prove. Questions that do not apply to your business are skipped. Open Admin → Fit interview and answer the questions. You can retake it any time. Choose Save answers and show the recommendation . Read What we suggest : how deep an implementation plan to follow, which features to show (each with the reason), which are worth considering, which are probably not needed yet, and anything that is not a fit yet. Optionally, choose Hide the features we did not recommend . This is reversible from the Features page. Hiding a feature removes it from everyone's menu, so check the list before you do it. If you are wondering why your colleagues are missing a menu entry, this and the Features page are the usual causes. See Why some menu items are missing . The interview, features and the implementation plan work together. See Administrator brief: your first week , features and editions and the implementation planner . Common mistakes Expecting your settings to change a colleague's screen. They are personal. Setting text to Larger and compact spacing together. It can crowd tables; try Roomy . Looking for these under your browser. They are held by the platform, so they follow your account, not one browser.

title: News, people and policies
text: The Company section of the menu is the everyday intranet: News and events , People and Policies & handbook . Everyone can read them. A few roles can write them. ( Improvements has its own page .) News and events This is the company noticeboard. Each item has a kind, which sets its label: News , Event , Safety , People or IT . An item is either for everyone or for one site, and may have an event date, which makes it appear under Coming up on Home. Pinned items stay at the top. The latest four items also show on Home . Reading Open Company → News and events for the full list. Each item shows its kind, date, author and site (or “everyone”), and the date of the event if it has one. Bodies can include headings, lists and bold text. Posting an announcement People who post announcements: HR managers and plant managers in the starter roles, and administrators. Open News and events . The form Post an announcement is at the top. Type a Headline and the Message . Use ## Heading for a heading, - item for a list and **bold** for bold. Choose the kind, and who it is for: Everyone or one site. Optionally set an Event date , a Show until date, and Pin to the top . Tick Also send a notification if people should be pinged. This is ticked and fixed on for Safety items, so safety notices always notify. Choose Post . To take one down, choose Withdraw next to it; it stays in the list for posters, marked Withdrawn . Posters also keep the Quick links on the home page at the bottom: add a title and an address (a full web address, or a path inside the platform that starts with / ), or Remove a link. People Company → People is the company directory: everyone, with work contact details only: name, job title, department, site and office, work email and work phone. Type a name, job, team or site in the box and choose Search (or use Find a colleague on Home). The count above the cards says how many people match. Click an email address to start a message, or a phone number to call from a phone. The directory shows only what a work directory needs. Private HR details are not included and stay with people who manage employee records. To correct your own entry, ask HR. Policies and the handbook Company → Policies & handbook holds the rules the company works by. It has three tabs. Employee handbook The handbook sections in order, with a contents list. Sections you have not yet acknowledged, because they are new or changed, carry a New tag. All policies Every policy that applies to you, with its number, title, kind (Handbook, Expenses, HR, IT, Safety, Quality, Finance, Other), the site it applies to, the revision in force and your status. Expense rules The current limits and receipt rules. See below. Reading and acknowledging Some policies require you to confirm that you have read them. When one is published or changed in a way that needs a fresh confirmation, you get a notification, and it shows under Policies to read and acknowledge on Home. Open Policies & handbook → All policies and look for To acknowledge in the You column, or open the handbook. Read the policy. For the handbook, a banner says how many sections are new or changed since you last acknowledged. Choose I have read this policy (on a policy) or I have read the handbook (in the handbook). The tag changes to Acknowledged with the date. You see Meaning To acknowledge You must read and confirm. Acknowledged You have confirmed the version in force. For reference Published for information; no confirmation needed. Not published Still a draft, visible only to people who write policies. A policy that is only slightly reworded (a “minor change”) keeps earlier acknowledgements. A substantive change asks everyone to confirm again. Expense rules The Expense rules tab shows what expense reports are checked against: the amount above which an itemized receipt is required, the mileage rate per mile (it says “a rate the company has not set yet” until one exists), the number of days within which expenses should be submitted, and, per category, the limit per expense, the limit per day and the receipt threshold, plus which categories also need to know who attended and why. The same table appears inside the expense and travel policy, so there is one source of truth. Writing and publishing policies Writing policies and the handbook, setting the expense rules, and seeing who has acknowledged is for HR managers, payroll administrators and administrators (the “manage policies” right). Everyone reads published policies. On All policies , under Add a policy , type a title, choose the kind and choose Add . Or choose Add missing template sections (or Start from templates on an empty handbook) to create draft handbook sections and an expense and travel policy. Templates are not legal advice; have them reviewed. Open the policy. Choose Edit draft (or Start a new revision for a published one) and write the text. Text in [[double brackets]] marks what your company still has to fill in. For a new revision, say what changed, and tick Minor change (wording only): keep earlier acknowledgements if it does not need re-confirming. Choose Save draft . When no placeholders are left, the page says Ready to publish . Pick an Effective date if you want, and choose Publish . Publish stays off while any placeholder remains. Track Acknowledgements on the policy: how many have confirmed and who is outstanding. History shows every revision, who published it and what changed. On the Expense rules tab, writers can edit the receipt threshold, the mileage rate and the submit-within days, and each category's limits. A policy can apply to everyone or to one site. Hiding Policies and handbook , News and events or People directory from a role is done under Admin → Features . See Administrator brief: features and editions . Common mistakes Expecting ordinary news to ping people. Only safety items, and items where Also send a notification is tick

title: Improvements
text: The Improvements page ( Company → Improvements ) is for ideas that make work safer, cheaper, faster or simpler. Anyone can suggest one. A lead approves it and names an owner; the owner measures how things were before , makes the change, measures after , and someone else checks the savings before it is closed. The aim is to count real results, not hopes. Everyone with a login can suggest an improvement. Leads (maintenance managers, plant managers, production supervisors, quality managers, executives and administrators in the starter roles) decide on ideas and validate savings. The owner a lead names carries the idea out. Suggest an improvement Open Company → Improvements and choose Suggest an improvement . Choose the Site it relates to and a Category (Safety, Quality, Cost, Delivery, Maintenance, Energy, Workplace or Other). Give it a short Title , such as “Shadow board for press tools”. In Problem , say what goes wrong today and how often. Facts and numbers help the lead decide. In Idea , say how you would fix it. This is optional. Choose Send . The idea gets a number and leads at that site are notified. When it is decided, you are told whether it was approved or not taken forward, with the lead's note. The list shows four counts at the top: ideas waiting, in progress, closed, and the validated savings per year so far. Click any row to open the improvement. The stages The bar at the top of each improvement shows where it is. Stage Meaning Who moves it on Idea Suggested; waiting for a decision. A lead chooses Approve (and names an Owner ) or Decline (a note is required). Approved Accepted, with an owner. The plan and the baseline are still to do. The owner or a lead. Baseline set The “before” measurement exists. The owner or a lead chooses The change is in place (today) . Implemented, measuring The change is made; the “after” is being measured. The owner measures the result; a different lead validates the savings. Closed Savings validated. The idea is finished. — Not taken forward Declined, with a reason. — Carry an improvement through (owners and leads) 1. Decide Open an improvement at stage Idea . Under Decision choose the owner and optionally add a note. Choose Approve , or write why not in the note and choose Decline . The owner is notified. 2. Plan how to measure it Under Measure , choose What is measured : Unplanned downtime of an asset (from records) : pick the asset. The system measures from its recorded downtime. Scrap rate at a work center (from records) : pick the work center. The system measures from production records. Something else, entered by hand : name the metric and its unit, and say whether lower is better. You type the baseline and the result. Optionally set a Target , an Est. savings / yr and a One-time cost . Choose Save the plan . Once a baseline is recorded, the kind of measurement can no longer be changed, so the before and after stay comparable. 3. Measure the baseline Choose Measure the baseline (last 8 weeks) for a measurement from records, or enter a value and choose Record the baseline for a hand-entered one. The first shows the date window it used. You can measure it again before the change is made. 4. Make the change Do the work. Add the next steps under Actions (an owner and a due date each) so they show up in the owner's My actions on Home. When the change is in place, choose The change is in place (today) . It cannot be dated in the future, nor before the baseline window. 5. Measure the result For a measurement from records, the system makes you wait at least four weeks after the change so a good week is not mistaken for a result. Until then the page says when the result can be measured. Choose Measure the result (or enter a value for a hand-entered metric). The page shows before, target, after, the percentage change, and whether the target was met. 6. Validate the savings A lead who is not the owner enters the Validated savings / yr and a note on how it was worked out, then chooses Validate and close . Savings of 0 are allowed. The improvement shows who validated it, when and how. Only validated savings count toward the total at the top of the list; estimates are shown in grey as “est.”. Common mistakes A vague problem. “Press is slow” gives a lead nothing to decide on. Say what, where and how often. Skipping the baseline. Without a before, there is nothing to compare. The system will not let you mark the change in place until the baseline is recorded. Owner validating their own savings. Not allowed; ask another lead. Measuring too early. The four-week wait is deliberate. Not seeing the menu entry. Improvements may be hidden for your role by your company. See why some menu items are missing . Improvements can be switched on or off per role under Admin → Features (see Administrator brief: features and editions ). Measuring downtime and scrap from records needs those records to exist: assets with recorded states, and production entries with scrap. The Improvements report appears under Reports .

title: Assets
text: An asset is any piece of equipment you look after: a machine, a vehicle, a building space, a tool. Each has one record that collects its details, its documents, its open work, its maintenance plans and its track record. Start here when something is wrong with a machine, or when you want to know how a machine has behaved. Who can do this: anyone with access to assets can search and read records. Technicians, maintenance managers, facilities managers and district managers can change a machine's state and record meter readings. Operators, technicians and most managers can report a problem. Maintenance managers and facilities managers can edit the repair-or-replace inputs and the spare-parts list. See Roles and access . Find an asset Open Maintenance → Assets . The page is titled Equipment register . Type in Search . You can search by tag, name, model or serial number. Optionally pick a Current state to narrow the list. Click a row to open the asset. The list shows site, tag, name, location, criticality, state and the number of open work orders. If you scan the QR code on a machine with your phone or tablet, it opens the same asset page directly. What the states mean An asset is always in one operational state. The state drives the downtime figures in the reports , so keep it honest. State Meaning Running Making product or doing its job. Available Ready to use. A machine returns to this state when a work order is verified. Idle Working, but nothing is scheduled for it. Planned downtime Stopped on purpose: maintenance, changeover, a holiday. Unplanned downtime Stopped because something went wrong. This counts as a failure. Out of service Taken out of use. Change a machine's state Open the asset. Under Details , click Running , Idle , Down (unplanned) or Planned stop . The button for the current state is greyed out. The page records when the state started. You cannot set Available or Out of service with these buttons; Available comes from verifying a work order (see Work orders ). Report a problem Open the asset and find the Report a problem box. Under What is wrong? , describe the symptom in a sentence or two (at least three characters). Pick a Severity : Low, Medium, High or Critical. Tick Machine is down if it has stopped. Click Send request . This does not create a work order straight away. It sends a request to maintenance, who turn it into a work order or decline it. See Work orders: requests . What is on an asset page Details : class, manufacturer and model, serial number, criticality, in-service date, current state and how long it has been in it, plus any custom fields your company added. Change banner : if a change request affects this asset, a yellow bar names it, with a link. Temporary changes show their end date. See Changes and notices . Technical documents : approved manuals and procedures linked to the asset, with an Open link. A document with no approved version shows No approved version . See Document control . Reliability : described below. Preventive maintenance : the plans for this asset, and a place to record meter readings (only if the PM feature is on). Spare parts : the parts that belong on this machine and how many you have at the site. Repair templates : stock repair jobs with their labor hours and parts. Open work orders and Components : the child assets that belong to this one. Record a meter reading Meters (run hours, cycles, miles) trigger meter-based preventive maintenance . On the asset page, go to Preventive maintenance . Type or pick the Meter name. If the asset has a meter plan, its meter name is suggested. Enter the Reading (the total on the meter, not the change since last time). Click Record meter reading . A message tells you how much is left before the next plan is due. Reliability The Reliability card shows failures, mean time between failures (MTBF), mean time to repair (MTTR) and availability for the last 30, 90 or 365 days, with a month-by-month table. A failure is an unplanned stop. MTBF is uptime divided by failures. MTTR is unplanned downtime divided by failures. A note under the figures says where the numbers came from: from state history (best), or estimated from work orders when nobody recorded states, or no data . If state records cover only part of the period, the page tells you how much. Failure codes that repeat within 30 days appear in red. Good reliability numbers depend on people pressing the state buttons and on technicians completing work orders with a failure code. A machine with no state history still gets estimates, but they are rougher. Repair or replace For machines and vehicles (not components or spaces), the Repair or replace card compares the yearly cost of keeping the asset (maintenance plus the cost of unplanned downtime, for this asset and its components) with the equivalent yearly cost of a new one. It shows one of three verdicts: Keep , Replace or Not enough data , with the reason in a sentence, the year replacing starts to pay, and a table by year. Click Edit the inputs . Enter the Replacement cost , the Expected life (years) and the Downtime cost / h . Without a downtime cost, the downtime column shows a dash and is left out of the comparison. Click Save . This is a guide, not a decision. It uses full years only, and it leaves out resale value, energy, safety and parts availability. Use it to start the conversation about capital spending. Common mistakes Reporting a problem and expecting a work order. A request only becomes a work order when a maintenance planner accepts it. Leaving a machine in Unplanned downtime after it is fixed. Verifying the work order does this for you; if you fixed it without a work order, press Running . Entering a meter reading as the amount since last time. Enter the reading on the meter. Administrators: people who may manage assets get a New asset button on this page (site, tag, name, kind, criticality, make, model and serial number; the rest is added on the asset page). Large numbers of

title: Work orders
text: A work order is one job on one asset: what is wrong or what must be done, who does it, which parts and hours it used, and who checked it afterward. Every maintenance job in the system, whether a breakdown, a scheduled preventive task or a contractor visit, follows the same life cycle. Request a job : operators, technicians, store managers and most managers (permission "request work orders"). Create, assign, schedule, cancel, close, dispatch contractors : maintenance managers, facilities managers, district managers (permission "manage work orders"). A service dispatcher also holds it. Start work, add labor and parts, mark complete : maintenance technicians and managers (permission "execute work orders"). Verify : maintenance managers, facilities managers, district managers, store managers (permission "verify work orders"). From a request to a work order Planners and managers can also start a job directly: click New work order at the top of the list, choose the asset, give it a title, type, priority and optional due date, and click Create work order . The rest of this section covers the usual route, through a request. Most jobs begin as a request. Anyone can send one from an asset page ( Assets: report a problem ), and the site's public request link, if your company uses one, adds requests from outside. Requests wait in an inbox for a planner. Open Maintenance → Work orders and click Requests . (You only see this button if you can manage work orders.) Read the request: when it arrived, the site and asset, the problem, who sent it, and the severity. Down and Safety flags show in red. Critical and high requests are highlighted. Click Create work order . A short form appears with a title (taken from the problem) and a priority set from the severity. Adjust the title and priority ( 1 Emergency , 2 High , 3 Normal , 4 Low ) and click Create . The new work order opens. If the request said the machine was down, the machine is put into unplanned downtime counted from when it was reported (unless its state has changed since). If you cannot act on a request, click Decline , give a reason (duplicate, not a maintenance issue) and click Decline request . Preventive maintenance creates its own work orders. See Preventive maintenance . Field service visits get one automatically; see Field service . The work order list The list has four views: Open , Assigned to me (if you are linked to an employee record), All and Requests . Each row shows the number, site, asset, title, priority, type, status, contractor, service-level pills and due date. Overdue jobs are marked in red. What the statuses mean Status Meaning Who moves it on Planned Created, not yet scheduled. Planner can schedule, hold or cancel. A technician can start work. Scheduled Booked for a time. Same as planned. In progress Work has started. Technician can hold it or mark it complete. On hold Paused, for example waiting on a part. Technician can resume; planner can reschedule or cancel. Completed The technician says the work is done. Not yet checked. Someone with verify permission verifies it or sends it back. Verified Checked by a second person. The machine returns to service. Planner closes it. Closed Finished and filed. No further changes. Cancelled Dropped. No further changes. Open a work order and do the work Click any row to open the work order. The Next step card shows the one action available to you now, plus the description and any safety notes in a yellow box. Click Start work . The system checks that everyone assigned still holds the qualifications the machine requires, and refuses if not. Record your time with Labor (below) and parts with Parts (below) as you go. When done, fill in the form: Work done and Findings . For corrective (breakdown) jobs, What fixed it? (required) must be filled in. Click Mark work complete . At least one labor entry must exist first (or a contractor's completion). Assign people On the work order, find the People card. In Assign a technician… , pick an active employee at the site and click Assign . The system refuses if the person lacks a qualification the machine requires. You can assign until the work is completed. The new assignee is notified. Record labor While the job is In progress or On hold , use the row under Labor . Pick the Work date and enter Hours (in quarter-hours, up to 24). Click Add my hours . Hours are added under your name. You must be linked to an employee record to see the form. The card total shows hours and labor cost. Record parts While the job is In progress , use the form under Parts . Choose a part. Parts planned for this job are listed first with a star. If your site stocks the part, choose the storeroom in Taken from… . Storerooms with nothing on hand are greyed out. Enter the quantity and click Record use . Stocked parts come out of that storeroom's balance. A part that is not stocked at this site is recorded without a stock movement. To put unused parts back, click Return on the line, enter how many, and confirm. You can return until the job is closed. Kits and repair templates The Kit card helps the storeroom prepare parts in advance. A planner can apply a repair template (a stock list of parts and hours for a known job), then click Build kit from planned parts to reserve the stock. The storeroom stages the kit; the technician clicks Issue kit to this job , and later Return unused and close kit . If a kit is still reserved or staged when the job is completed or cancelled, the reservation is released automatically. Parts you do not have If planned parts exceed what has been used, a Purchasing card offers Request parts not in stock (for people who may raise purchase requests). It shows each request and order, expected dates and what has arrived. See Purchasing . Send a job to a contractor On an open work order, click Send to a contractor in the Contractor card. Optionally type a Trade to filter, choose the contractor, and set a Not to exceed ($) limit and a no

title: Preventive maintenance
text: Preventive maintenance (PM) is routine work done on a schedule: lubricate every month, change filters every 500 run hours. A PM plan says what to do, on which asset, how often, and which parts it needs. When a plan comes due, the system makes a normal work order for it. Who can do this: anyone who can view work orders can see the schedule and the plans. Maintenance managers, facilities managers and district managers can create plans, pause or resume them, and generate work orders (permission "manage work orders"). Technicians and operators with meter access can record meter readings from the asset page. Where to find it Open Maintenance → PM . If you do not see it, your company has the preventive maintenance feature turned off, or you lack access to work orders. The PM schedule The page shows plans due now or in the next 60 days. Four counters across the top summarise the state of play: Overdue : plans past their due date or reading. Due now : plans inside their lead window. Due without a work order : due or overdue plans nobody has started a job for. Short of parts : plans whose parts list is not fully in stock at the site. The table lists plan code, site, asset, interval, next due, state, the current work order (if any) and a parts check ( In stock or N short ). Overdue rows are marked red. State Meaning Not due The due date or reading is still beyond the lead window. Due Inside the lead window. It is time to plan the job. Overdue The due date has passed, or the meter has reached the due reading. Paused The plan has been switched off. It does not generate work orders. Calendar plans and meter plans Calendar Due every N days. It is due from the due date minus the lead window in days. Meter reading Due every N units of a meter (run hours, cycles). It is due once the latest recorded reading reaches the due reading minus the lead amount. Readings are entered on the asset page; see Assets: record a meter reading . The plan also has a schedule basis : Count from when work is done The next due point is one interval after the work is finished. A late job pushes everything back. Keep fixed dates The next due point is one interval after the previous due point , skipping any cycle you have already passed. Dates keep their rhythm even when a job runs late. Create a plan On the PM page, click New plan . Choose the Asset . Give it a Plan code that is unique (for example PM-CNC-102-M ) and a Title . Choose the Trigger : Calendar or Meter reading . For a calendar plan, enter Every (days) . For a meter plan, enter the Meter name and Every (meter units) . Optionally set the First due date (or first due reading). If you leave it blank, the first due point is one interval from now. Choose the Schedule basis (see above). Enter Estimated hours if you know them. Under Parts list , click Add a part for each part and quantity the job uses. Click Create plan . The plan opens. Use the same meter name every time (for example always run_hours ). The asset page suggests the meter names already in use. Generate work orders Work orders from PM are made when you ask for them, not automatically in the background. On the PM page, click Generate due work orders . A green message lists what was created (work order number and plan), and which plans were skipped because they already have an open work order. Generation makes one work order per due plan and never a duplicate. Each is a preventive work order titled "PM: ..." with the plan's parts planned on it. If the parts are stocked at the site, the stock is reserved in a kit so it is waiting when work starts. Technicians then work the job as usual. The plan only moves forward when its work order is verified , not when it is completed. If nobody verifies, the plan stays due and, once the job is closed, will be due again. See Work orders: verify . A plan's page Click a plan to see its schedule: trigger and basis, next due, lead window, last done (date and reading), estimated time and procedure document. Beside it is the parts list with On hand at site and a Short flag. Below is the history of work orders from the plan, each marked On time or Late . Pause or resume a plan Open the plan. Type a reason in the box (at least five characters, for example "asset idle until Q1"). Click Pause plan (or Resume plan when it is paused). The reason is kept in the audit trail. Common mistakes Waiting for work orders to appear on their own. Press Generate due work orders regularly, or rely on the reminder (below). Forgetting to enter meter readings. A meter plan with no reading yet never becomes due. Completing the work order but never verifying it, so the plan does not advance. Planning a part that is not stocked at the site. The plan shows not stocked , and the job's kit is not built. Administrators: a daily reminder, "PM plans due without a work order", goes to maintenance planners at the site when a plan is inside its lead window and has no open work order. You can change or turn it off under Reminders and retention . The whole PM area can be hidden under Features and editions .

title: Storerooms
text: Storerooms hold your spare parts. Every change to a quantity, whether a receipt, an issue to a work order, a return, a transfer, an adjustment or a count, is written to a ledger, so you can always see how a balance came about. This page shows stock by storeroom and is where you receive, adjust, count and track lots. Who can do this: anyone with stock access (technicians, buyers, managers) can view stock, the ledger, lots and kits. Maintenance managers and others with "manage inventory" can receive parts, post adjustments, set reorder levels, run counts, put lots on hold and map barcodes. Issuing parts to a work order only needs the right to work on that job. Changing a part's tracking or units needs "manage parts" (maintenance managers and buyers). Open Maintenance → Storerooms . There are four tabs: Stock , Lots , Kits and Cycle counts . For barcode work on a tablet see Scan station . Stock on hand Four counters sit at the top: Stocked lines , At or below reorder point , Out of stock and Stock value (at average cost). Below, search by part number or description, or tick Only at or below reorder point . A row shows storeroom, part, bin, on-hand quantity, reorder level and last movement, with an Out or Reorder badge where needed. See how a balance came about Click a stock row. A panel opens for that part at that storeroom. Read the movements: when, type, quantity (+ or -), balance after, reference (work order, packing slip or reason) and who did it. Receive parts Use this for stock arriving without going through a purchase order. If you have a purchase order, receive against it so the order stays accurate; see Purchasing or the scan station . On the Stock tab, scroll to Receive parts . Choose the Storeroom and the Part . Enter the Quantity . Optionally add Unit cost (USD) and a Packing slip / PO reference. If the part is tracked, enter the lot (with an expiry date if it has one) or list the serial numbers, one per line. The page shows "N of M serial numbers" so you can check the count. Click Receive . A green message gives the new balance. You can split a delivery across lots with Split into another lot . The unit cost feeds the part's average cost. Issue parts Parts leave a storeroom in one of three ways: A technician records Record use on a work order and chooses the storeroom. See Work orders: record parts . A storeroom clerk issues a prepared kit to the job. See Kits . The Kits tab lists open kits needed by date, with any shortage flagged. The scan station issues by scanning to a work order or a job reference. Stock cannot go below zero. If a tracked part has several lots, the first to expire is used unless someone chooses another; lots on hold or past expiry are never issued. Adjust a balance Click the stock row to open the part panel. Under Adjust , enter Change (+ or -) and a Reason of at least five characters, such as "damaged in storage". For a tracked part, enter the lot or serial. It is required when adding, and optional when removing (blank means the first to expire). Click Post adjustment . For finding a difference on the shelf, a count is better than an adjustment: it records what you found and posts the difference for you. Reorder levels Open the part panel. Under Reorder settings , set the Reorder point and Reorder quantity . Click Save . A part at or below its reorder point is flagged Reorder and counted in the top counters. Buyers then raise a purchase request; see Purchasing . Units of measure A part is stocked and counted in one unit, shown in the Units section of the part panel. If it is bought in packs, boxes, cases or drums, someone with part-management rights can add a unit ("1 BOX = 100 EA"), so purchasing and receiving convert for you. A unit that a supplier is priced in cannot be removed. Counting stock Open the Cycle counts tab. It lists counts with storeroom, status, how many lines are counted, and when opened and posted. Choose a Storeroom to count… and click Start a count . A count sheet opens listing every part there, with bin and the expected quantity as of that moment. Count the shelf. Enter each Counted quantity. Click Save counts to keep your progress. If you find a tracked lot that is not on the sheet, use Found a lot that is not on the sheet to add it. When every line is counted, click Post count . A green message lists the differences, or "No variances." If stock moved while you counted, the page stops and says so. Click Post against current quantities to accept the moves and post the differences against today's numbers. Count status Meaning Open Still being counted. Counts can be saved and continued. Posted Differences have been written to the ledger. The sheet is read-only.
