A count started on the scan station is blind : expected quantities are hidden until it is posted, so the counter is not nudged toward the book figure. Lots and serial numbers A part can be tracked by lot (a batch, often with an expiry date) or by serial number (one unit each). The Lots tab lists tracked stock. Search by lot, serial, supplier lot or part, or use the filter: In stock , Expired or expiring within 30 days , or On hold . Lot status Meaning Available Can be issued or shipped. Expired Past its expiry date. Never issued or shipped. On hold Blocked, with a reason. Never issued or shipped. Scrapped Written off. Switch tracking on for a part Open the part panel from the Stock tab. Under Lot and serial tracking , choose By lot or By serial number . Optionally set a Shelf life in days, which fills in expiry dates on receipt. If stock is already on hand, enter a lot number (and expiry) for each storeroom's quantity so it can be put into a lot now. Click Save . To track by serial number, count the stock out to zero first (or track by lot). The page warns you if there is stock on hand. A lot's page Click a lot to see where it is, what it was made from, where it went (production orders, customer shipments, work orders) and every movement. Print label makes a barcode

title: Scan station
text: The scan station is a touch-friendly screen for the storeroom. You receive deliveries, issue parts to jobs and count shelves by scanning barcodes instead of typing. It posts exactly the same ledger entries as the typed screens on Storerooms ; it is simply faster and makes fewer mistakes. Who can do this: everyone with stock access can open the station and use Look up and Labels . Receive , Issue , Count and Barcodes need the "manage inventory" right (maintenance managers). Someone who can receive purchase orders (buyers) also sees Receive . Technicians with only view access see just the lookup and label tabs. What you need A tablet or computer with a browser, signed in to the system, with a connection. The station does not work offline. A USB or Bluetooth scanner that acts like a keyboard, which needs no setup. Or use the tablet's camera where the browser supports it. Or type the code and press Enter . Open Maintenance → Scan station . Across the top are the modes. A coloured banner under them confirms each scan, with a beep for success or failure. A wrong scan is refused with the reason, and nothing is posted. What the codes mean Whatever is scanned is looked up and recognised as one of these: Scan What it is L:CODE A storeroom location. The L: prefix is reserved for our location labels. LOT:PARTNUMBER:LOTNUMBER A lot or serial number. The LOT: prefix is reserved for our lot labels. A plain part number A part. Checked first. A supplier's UPC, EAN, carton or supplier code A part, if someone has mapped that code to it (see Barcodes ). A purchase order number A purchase order, if you may receive for that site. A work order number A work order, if you may view it. A plain location code A location. This works as a fallback when there is no L: prefix. The prefixes exist so a location code and a part number can never be mistaken for each other. Anything unrecognised is refused with "is not a part, location, lot, purchase order or work order here". Receive Choose the Receive tab. Scan the purchase order. The station shows the order's lines with ordered, received and to-come quantities. If there is no order, skip this step: the screen says "none (receiving without an order)". If there is no order, scan the shelf location . With an order, each line already knows its storeroom. Scan the part. Scanning the same part again adds to the quantity (one scan adds the part's "quantity per scan", normally 1). With an order, a part that is not an open line is refused. Check the quantity, using the minus and plus buttons if needed. For a lot- or serial-tracked part, enter the lot or serial number and, if it has one, the expiry date. Press Receive . The banner says what was received and how many lines are still open. With an order, the receipt is posted against it; without, it is a plain receipt with the reference "Scan receipt". Quantities are limited to what is still to come on the line. Press Clear order to start again. Issue Choose the Issue tab. Scan the storeroom location you are taking from. Scan the work order , or type a job, cost centre or line in Job, cost centre or line if there is no work order. Scan the part. The banner shows how many are on hand at that location, and turns red if none are. Check the quantity, then press Issue . Issuing to a work order records the part on that job, with labor and cost, the same as Record use on the work order. Issuing to a reference is a plain stock issue. The station does not issue lot- or serial-tracked parts: it tells you to issue those from the work order or the storeroom screen, where the lot is chosen. Count Choose the Count tab. The Due for counting table lists storerooms with parts due by schedule. Either press Count these (or Continue ) beside a storeroom, or scan a shelf location to start or continue a count there. Scan each part. Enter what is on the shelf with the plus and minus buttons or by typing. For a tracked part, choose the lot or serial number. Press Save count . The list Still to count shrinks as you go. When it is empty, press Finish and post . If you must stop, press Leave it open and continue later. Counts from the station are blind : the screen does not show the expected quantity, so you count what you see. When posted, the banner lists any differences ("Posted. 2 differences: ...") or says everything matched. If stock moved during the count, a red button appears: Stock moved during the count: post against current quantities . The count schedule A part at a storeroom can be given a count interval in days (up to three years). It becomes due when it has never been counted, or the last count was longer ago than the interval. The station groups the due parts by storeroom. "Count these" opens a count containing only what is due. If nothing is listed, no part has an interval set. Set it in Maintenance → Storerooms : open the part at its storeroom and fill in Count every (days) under Reorder and counting settings . Leave it blank to take the part off the schedule. Look up Scan anything on the Look up tab to see what it is. For a part you get description, unit, whether it is tracked, and where it is on hand. For a location, its code and name (and an Inactive badge if closed). For a lot, its status and expiry. For an order or work order, its status and open lines. Labels Open the Labels tab. Choose Label for Storeroom locations or Parts . Tick the rows you want. Press Print N labels . A PDF opens. Print it on Avery 5160 label sheets (30 per page, three across). Location labels carry the L: code; part labels carry the plain part number. Lot and serial labels are printed from the lot's own page (see Storerooms: a lot's page ). A code that cannot be printed as a barcode (letters, digits and punctuation only, up to 48 characters) is refused with a message. Barcodes Suppliers' cartons often have their own barcode. Map it once and it scans as your part. Open the Barcodes tab and choose a Part . Enter the Code (3 to 60 characters), the Kind (UPC, E

title: Field service
text: Field service is for companies whose business is maintaining other people's equipment on a schedule. A customer signs a service agreement covering some equipment. The system generates visits on the agreed frequency. A coordinator (the dispatcher) assigns each visit to a technician. The technician does the work on a tablet (see Field service: My day ), and the visit is billed. Field service is licensed per site . If your site does not have the field service licence, the menu is hidden and the pages refuse to open. Ask your administrator; see the box at the end. Who can do this: a service dispatcher (permission "manage field service") can create call-outs and agreements, assign and unassign visits, send the day to a technician, cancel visits, and manage technicians, trucks and settings. Field technicians have "execute field service" and use My day. Managing billing and creating invoices needs receivables authority ("view receivables" to see the Billing tab and "manage receivables" to create invoices). Making quotes needs the right to quote (service dispatchers and sales representatives). Open Field service → Field service . The tabs are Dispatch , Visits , Agreements , Technicians, trucks and tools , Billing and Settings . Billing shows only to people with receivables access, and Settings only to dispatch managers. A Performance report button at the top opens the service report; see Reports . Agreements An agreement is a contract with one customer for one servicing site. It lists the units it covers and how often each is serviced. On the Agreements tab, click New agreement . Choose the Customer and Servicing site . Set Starts and (optionally) Ends . Choose Billing : Per visit (enter a fee per visit) or Flat monthly (enter a monthly fee). Optionally set the Response time for call-outs (hours) , tick Parts are included in the fee and Renews automatically , and add Terms . Click Save draft . On the agreement, under Add a covered unit , choose the equipment, name the service (for example "Quarterly PM"), set Every N weeks, months or years, the First due date, estimated minutes, any skill needed, a checklist (one item per line) and, if different, a fee for this unit. Click Add . Click Activate (generates the visits) . At least one unit must be covered. Equipment must already belong to the customer. Visits are created ahead of time (30 days by default, see Settings ), one per plan and date. If a plan fell behind, you get one overdue visit, not a pile. Agreement status Meaning Draft Being set up. No visits yet. Active Visits are being generated. Suspended Paused with a reason. Activate resumes it. Ended Finished normally, with a reason. Cancelled Cancelled, with a reason. Suspend , End and Cancel each need a reason of at least three characters. To stop covering one unit use Remove beside it, and Restore to bring it back. Call-outs A call-out is an unscheduled visit for a breakdown. On the Visits tab, click New call-out . Choose the Customer , then the Equipment (add new equipment to the customer first). Set Priority , Needed by , Minutes and any Skill needed . Describe What is wrong and add notes. Click Create call-out . The visit appears under To schedule on the dispatch board with a Call-out tag. Visits and their statuses The Visits tab lists visits (filter Open visits , Overdue or All ). Click one to open it. Status Meaning To schedule Exists, not yet assigned. Scheduled Assigned to a technician on a day. The technician has been told. Dispatched The day has been sent to the technician. On site The technician started the visit. Done The service report was submitted. Cancelled Cancelled with a reason. An Overdue tag appears when the due date has passed. To cancel a visit that is not yet started, type a reason (at least three characters) and click Cancel visit . The dispatch board The Dispatch tab shows one day. Use the arrows, the date or Today to change day. There is one card per technician, showing: How full the day is as a percentage (green, amber over 85%, red if overbooked), or why they are not working (for example time off). Their skills, and minutes on site plus minutes driving against the day's capacity. Their stops: arrival time, visit, customer and site, and drive minutes. Under the cards, To schedule lists visits with no technician in the next week, with customer, what, due date, minutes and skill. Assign a visit In To schedule , click Assign… on a visit. A panel ranks the technicians. For each you see Can take it or the reasons they cannot (missing skill, not working that day, time off, too many booked hours), Extra drive , visits already that day and minutes free afterward. Click Assign beside a technician who can take it. Assigning creates the visit's work order , assigns the technician to it and notifies them. The system picks a start time: after the technician's previous stop plus drive time, or the start of their day. It refuses a visit that would run past the end of the day. To undo, click Unassign on the stop; it goes back to To schedule . Send the day When a technician's day is right, click Send the day to NAME . All their scheduled visits for that day change to Dispatched . How drive time is estimated The system does not use a maps service. Drive time is the straight-line distance between stops multiplied by a road factor , divided by an average speed . Both are typed in Settings (the note above the board shows the current values). A stop with a star after the minutes is an estimate because a site or technician has no map coordinates; the system then assumes 20 minutes. Treat all drive times as a guide for ranking people, not a promise to the customer. Technicians, trucks and tools Technicians : shows name, skills, working hours, truck and visits today. A dispatcher turns an employee into a technician by choosing them, entering Skills (comma separated) and optional home latitude and longitude, and clicking Save technician . Trucks : add a vehicle with a tag, name

title: Field service: My day
text: My day is the screen a field technician uses on a tablet in the truck and at the customer's site. It shows your stops for the day in order, with the time to arrive, the customer's address, access notes and the equipment. When you start a visit you fill in the service report. Submitting it completes the job and sends it for billing. Who can do this: field technicians (permission "execute field service"). You must also be set up as a technician by your dispatcher, or the page says "You are not set up as a technician. Ask your dispatcher." Field service must be licensed for your site. Open Field service → My day . Your dispatcher's side of this is described in Field service . Your route Use the arrows or the date box to move between days. Each stop is a card showing: The arrival time and customer, and the status of the stop (scheduled, dispatched, in progress or completed). What the job is and the equipment tag and name. The site and address, drive time from the previous stop (marked "estimate" if the system could not use map coordinates), and the expected minutes on site. Access notes in a yellow box, for example where to park or who to ask for. The make, model and serial number of the equipment. "Nothing is scheduled for you on this day" means you have no visits assigned. You are told in the app when a visit is assigned to you. Start a visit Find the stop. Its button says Start the visit while it is scheduled or dispatched. Tap Start the visit when you arrive. The report form opens and the stop turns to in progress . Once a visit is in progress, the button on the card reads Service report (or Hide the report when the form is open). A finished stop shows View report . Fill in the service report Work from the top of the form to the bottom. Everything is large enough to use with a finger. Checklist. If the visit has a checklist, tap OK , Issue or N/A for every item. For an Issue , type what is wrong. You must answer every item before you can submit. Readings. Tap Add a reading for measurements such as amps or pressure. Give the name, the value and the unit. Work performed. Describe what you did (at least five characters). This is required. Findings. Anything you noticed. Hours on site. Enter hours in quarter-hour steps. This is required and must be more than zero and no more than 24. The problem is fixed. On a call-out, tick this when you solved it. Parts used (from the truck). Tap Add a part , choose the part and quantity. Parts come off your truck's stock, and cannot go below zero. Other work the customer needs. Tap Add a recommended repair for anything else you found. Describe it, choose Now , Soon or When convenient , and enter a price if you know it. Each becomes a line on a draft quote that the office can send. Customer sign-off. If the customer is there, leave The customer is here to sign ticked, type their name and have them sign in the box. If they are not, untick it and say why (not on site, refused, locked out). Tap Submit report . Tap Save draft at any point. The draft is kept on the server (or, with no connection, on the tablet and sent later) and also on the tablet as you type. When you reopen the report, after a reload, a closed tab or on another tablet, your entries are put back in the form: checklist answers, readings, work performed, findings, hours, parts, recommended repairs and the signature. The page says Draft restored . About the signature If the customer is present, both a typed name (at least two characters) and a drawn signature are required. If they are not, a short reason is required instead. The signature image is stored with the report and shown to the office as View signature . A signature saved with a draft stays with it when you reopen the report; draw again only to replace it. Without a connection My day keeps working when the signal drops, in a basement or at a remote site. While you are online the tablet keeps a copy of your day, of each visit's details and report draft, and of the parts list. Open My day once with a connection before you set off. See the day and the details. The page says Copy saved on this device [time]: no connection right now . Visit details opens the number, customer, agreement, due date, access notes, notes and checklist of a stop. Start a visit. Start the visit works as usual: the stop turns to in progress with a Waiting to send tag, and the time you tapped is kept as your arrival time. Fill in the report. Labor hours, parts, notes, readings, findings, recommended repairs and the customer's signature all work. Save draft says Draft saved on this device . The form checks the same things the server will (every checklist item answered, work performed, hours, name and signature or a reason) so a missing item is shown at once and not hours later. Submit. Submit report closes the form and shows the stop as completed and waiting to send. The visit is not billed and the office does not see the report until it is sent. Each change waits in order (start, draft, submission) and goes to the server when the connection returns, on its own, within a minute. Each carries a unique key, so if the network dropped just as a change went through, sending it again changes nothing a second time: the labor and parts are posted once. See Working offline and on tablets for the outbox. If the server refuses a change (the dispatcher cancelled or reassigned the visit, the truck did not have enough of a part), the stop shows Refused with the reason. Choose Correct the report to reopen the form with your entries still in it, fix it and submit again (the new attempt replaces the refused one), choose Try again if the cause is gone, or Discard to drop it. Nothing is dropped silently. What happens when you submit Your hours are recorded as labor on the visit's work order. Your parts are taken off your truck's stock and recorded on the work order. Checklist items marked Issue are added to the findings. The work order is marked completed. A second person with veri

title: Staffing and utilization
text: Service companies → Staffing answers three questions: who is planned on which project, who has room (or too much), and how much of people's available time turns into billable work. It uses working hours, holidays, time off, the assignments you make, and approved timesheets. Everyone with an employee record sees their own capacity and utilization, and the people who report to them (through the manager set on the employee record). Operations managers, HR managers, executives and district managers can see the people at their sites. Operations managers and HR managers (and administrators) can change assignments, working patterns, holidays, targets and decide time off, at the sites where they hold the permission. Company-wide settings need the permission at all sites. The feature can be switched off or limited to roles under Admin → Features (Standard edition). The capacity grid The Capacity tab shows people down the side and weeks across. Each cell reads booked / available hours and says its state in words: State Meaning Over-allocated Booked hours are above available hours (by more than the tolerance set under Setup , half an hour unless changed). Fully booked Booked hours use up the available hours. Part booked Some hours are booked and some are free. Unbooked The person has hours available and nothing booked. Not working No available hours that week and nothing booked (for example a week of leave). Colour reinforces the words; it is never the only signal. The grid works from the keyboard: tab to a person's name or a cell and press Enter to open that person below the grid. Use the arrows to move the weeks, and the menus to narrow by site, department or manager. How available hours are worked out For each day: the person's working pattern for that weekday (or the company's default week when they have none), less any company holiday for their site, less approved time off. Field service technician time off counts as full days off. A person's own pattern starts on its date and stays until a later one starts. Assign people to projects Open a person from the grid and choose Add an assignment . Pick the project, give the hours a week, the dates and whether it is Tentative or Confirmed . Add a role and a note if useful. Whether the time is billable starts from the project: a non-billable project defaults to non-billable. Choose Check and add . If the booking would push any week over capacity, the page lists those weeks and still lets you Save anyway . The reason you type is kept with the assignment (shown as the conflict note). Hours a week are spread over the days the person works. A booking that starts on Wednesday counts the share of the week from Wednesday on. A company holiday shrinks the booking in proportion (a full-time booking in a holiday week is not a conflict). Personal time off does not shrink it, so a booked person who is away shows as over-allocated, which is the cue to move the work. Use Edit or move to change hours, dates, state, or to move the assignment to another person; Remove frees the hours. Every create, move, edit and removal is recorded; History shows who did what, with the conflict note. Projects at sites you do not manage cannot be used. Only projects that are not finished are offered. Utilization Utilization is billable hours divided by available hours, for a period you choose, grouped by person, department, manager, site or job title. Billable hours come only from approved timesheets (including those already sent to payroll), on time entries marked billable. Hours on submitted timesheets that are not approved yet are shown in their own column and are not counted. Only whole days that have passed count; the page says through which date. A person with no approved timesheet in the period has no utilization (shown as No approved time ), not 0%. Team figures include only people with approved time. When nobody has any, the page says so instead of showing zeros. Targets: a person's own target wins, then the target for their job title (matched to the job title on the employee record), then the company target (75% until changed). Team targets are weighted by available hours. People who are not staffed on projects (an owner, office staff) can be left out with Leave this person out on their page. They disappear from utilization, the bench report, the forecast and the reminders. Time off On the Time off tab you can ask for time off (whole days, or some hours a day). A manager with the permission at your site approves or rejects it; nobody decides their own. Approved time off reduces available hours. When a manager enters time off for someone else it is recorded as approved straight away. Managers are told of new requests; you are told of the decision. Setup The Setup tab (managers only) holds the default working week, the company target, the bench threshold (people booked under this share of capacity are on the bench), the overbooking tolerance, company holidays (for every site, or one site; whole day or some hours) and utilization targets. Individual working patterns are set on each person's page with Set a pattern . Holidays are not preloaded; add the ones your company observes each year. Targets by job title match the job title text on the employee record, ignoring capitals. Reports Under Insight → Reports (CSV, Excel and PDF as for other reports): Utilization : the table above, for the period and grouping you pick. Bench and overbooking : people booked below the bench threshold over the next weeks (four by default), and each over-allocated week. Staffing forecast : capacity against confirmed and tentative bookings for the next 13 weeks. It shows what is planned, not what will be sold. Reminders The daily job can tell staffing managers at each site about: people over-allocated next week, people with nothing booked in the next two weeks, and, on the last day of the month, people below their utilization target for the month. Each is a single summary per site and i

title: Production orders
text: A production order is an instruction to make a stated quantity of one part at one site, by a due date. It follows the part's released product revision: the list of materials per unit and the routing (the ordered operations, each at a work center). This page covers the Production menu's Orders , Products and Work centers tabs. Running the work on the floor is covered in Shop floor and shift log . See orders, products and work centers : anyone with "view production", such as operators, production supervisors, plant managers, quality staff and sales. Create and release orders, edit and release product revisions, add work centers, cancel, complete short, close : production supervisors/planners and plant managers (permission "manage production"). Issue materials, receive finished goods, start and stop runs : operators and production supervisors (permission "execute production"), for their own site. Request what is short : needs the purchasing request permission as well. Production is part of the Standard edition and can be switched off per company, so you may not see these pages. See the administrator note at the end. Where to find it Open Production → Production orders . Four tabs run across the top: Orders , Shop floor , Products and Work centers . The three tiles on the Orders tab show open orders, late orders and orders in progress. Tick Only open and completed to hide closed and cancelled orders. Late orders are marked in red. What the statuses mean Status Meaning What moves it on Planned The order exists but has no materials or operations yet. Quantity can still change. A manager releases it, or cancels it. Released Materials and operations were copied from the current released revision. The floor can see it. The first run started on the floor makes it In progress. A manager can still cancel it if no material has been issued. In progress At least one run has started. Receiving the full quantity completes it. A manager can complete it short. Completed The full quantity was received, or the order was completed short with a reason. A manager closes it. Closed Finished and filed. No further changes. — Cancelled Dropped, with a reason. No further changes. — A Late tag appears beside any planned, released or in-progress order whose due date has passed. Create an order On the Orders tab, click New production order . Choose Part to make… . Only parts with a released revision are offered, and the revision number is shown. Choose the Site , enter the Quantity , and optionally a due date. Choose Finished goods to… , the storeroom at that site where the made parts will go. You can leave it for later, but you cannot receive goods until it is set. Click Create . The order opens as Planned . If the part has no released revision, the order is refused. Start with the Products tab (below). Orders can also come from the plan: the Planned production table on the Planning page has a "create order" link for each part and month. Release it to the floor Open the planned order and click Release to the floor . The system copies the materials and operations from the part's current released revision. A message tells you whether all materials are covered, or lists the parts that are short. The order keeps the revision it was released with, even if a newer revision is released later. If the routing uses a work center at a different site, release is refused; make the order at that site instead. Materials: what is short, issuing, and making sub-assemblies The Materials table shows, for each part, the quantity required, issued so far, available at the site, and any shortage. Rows with a shortage are highlighted. A purchased part is short : click Request what is short . A purchase request is drafted for the shortfall, less what is already on order or already requested. It opens for you to review. See Purchasing . A part marked "made in house" is short : managers see a Make link beside the shortfall. It creates a new production order for the missing quantity, with the same due date. In the Materials table, enter the quantity under Issue now for each line. Choose the storeroom if more than one holds stock. For lot-tracked parts, choose the lot. Or click Fill remaining to propose the quantity still needed, up to what the first storeroom holds. Click Issue materials . The stock moves out of the storeroom onto the order and appears in Stock movements at the bottom of the page. Once some goods are finished, the Variance column shows how actual usage compares with the standard quantity. Operations and the shop-floor record The Operations table lists each step in order: work center, what is done, quantity received from the previous step, good, scrap and reworked counts, and minutes actual against standard. A linked work instruction opens in the document viewer (see Document control ). An operation cannot start until the previous one is finished. Operators normally start work from the Shop floor tab. If you are linked to an employee record and allowed to run production, a Start button also appears on the order itself and takes you to the right work center. The Shop-floor record lists every run with times, operator, machine, quantities and notes. For a run that scrapped parts, people who may report quality problems see Raise NCR , which opens a nonconformance already linked to the run (see Quality ). Return unused material The Materials table shows, for each line, what was Required , what was Issued to the order in total, what has been Returned , and, on a completed or closed order, what is Left over : issued and not returned, beyond what the good and scrapped units used at standard (quantity per unit with the line's scrap allowance). Click Return material under the table. It appears for people who may run production, on released, in-progress and completed orders that have material issued. Choose the material line, the Quantity (on a completed order it starts at the left-over amount; it cannot excee

title: Planning
text: The Planning page turns customer forecasts and firm sales orders into two answers. First, how loaded each work center will be, month by month, against the hours it can really deliver. Second, which purchased materials you will be short of, and the date by which you must order them. You can try "what if" scenarios without changing anything, and you can turn the plan into purchase requests and production orders with one click. See the plan and forecasts : plant managers, production supervisors/planners, buyers, sales staff and executives (permission "view planning"). Create scenarios, draft purchase requests, create production orders, activate forecasts, edit calendars and consumption rates : plant managers and production supervisors/planners (permission "manage planning"). Creating orders also needs the production manage permission; drafting a purchase request needs the purchasing request permission. Open Production → Planning . Pick the site in the box at the top right (only plant sites are listed). Tabs: Plan , Forecasts , and, for managers, Calendars and Consumables . Reading the Plan tab Choose a Horizon of 3, 6, 9 or 12 months. The tiles at the top summarise the plan: Peak load The busiest work center in the busiest month, as a percentage of its capacity. Work-center months over How many work center and month combinations need more than 100 percent of capacity. Materials short How many purchased parts you will not have enough of in the horizon. Operator shortfall Shown only when work centers require qualifications. Counts work-center months where there are not enough qualified people. Firm share of demand How much of the demand is firm sales orders rather than forecast. Work-center load Each cell shows a percentage and "hours needed / hours available". The colour shows how tight it is. Colour Load Meaning Green 85 percent or less Comfortable. Amber Over 85 up to 100 percent Tight. Little room for breakdowns or rush orders. Red Over 100 percent Overloaded. The plan cannot be met without more capacity or less demand. Hover over a cell to see the pieces: hours from open production orders, firm orders, forecast, and the capacity after preventive maintenance. A line under the work center name shows its hours per week, number of machines or crews, and availability. Load is open production orders plus planned production (firm and forecast), run through each part's released routing. Capacity is the calendar hours times the machines or crews, times the availability the machines have actually demonstrated (from their recorded state), less preventive maintenance hours projected from the machines' calendar PM plans. In each month, for a customer and part, the larger of the forecast and the firm orders counts, so firm orders above the forecast are never lost. Qualified operators If work centers require qualifications, a second table shows, per month, either "covered" or "N h short" of qualified people. A work center that depends on one person (or nobody) gets a tag. A list below names people whose qualification expires within the horizon and how many qualified people the work center will then have. People are shared: someone qualified on two work centers is counted once. See Training and performance . Materials The table lists each purchased part the plan needs, with the quantity available now, needed, on order, short, already requested, the date it is needed by, and the Order by date. A red past tag means the order-by date has already gone by. The For column says whether the demand comes from production, consumption (coolant, inserts, chemicals) or preventive maintenance parts. Turning the plan into action These buttons appear only for the plan "as planned", never when a scenario is selected, and only if you have the permissions above. To buy what is short, click Draft a purchase request for N short materials above the Materials table. A draft request opens for you to review and submit for approval. The shortfalls already requested or on order are not repeated. See Purchasing . To make something, find the part and month in the Planned production table and click create order . A planned production order is created. Release it when you are ready. See Production orders . Try a scenario A scenario changes the plan on screen without changing any real data. Use it to ask "what if demand rises 15 percent" or "what if we add a second shift on the lathes". Click New scenario . Give it a name, for example "Second shift on lathes". Enter a Forecast change in percent (for example 15 or -10). Optionally pick a work center and enter extra hours per week and extra machines or crews. Click Save and show . The tiles now show the new peak load and note what it was before. Choose As planned (no scenario) in the scenario box to go back to the real plan. Assumptions the plan made If the plan had to guess, for example a work center without a calendar, it lists the guesses under Assumptions this plan had to make . Read this before relying on the numbers. Forecasts The Forecasts tab lists the customer forecasts for the site: customer, version, status, months covered, total quantity, date received and source. Click one to see the quantities per part and month. Each cell shows the change from the version before it, and the firm sales-order quantity in that month. A red "firm" figure means firm orders already exceed the forecast. Status Meaning Draft Imported but not yet used by the plan. Active The version the plan uses for that customer. Superseded An earlier version, replaced when a newer one was activated. Kept for history. Import the customer's forecast (see the administrator note). Open the new draft and compare it with the previous version. Managers click Use this version in the plan . Calendars (managers) For each work center, set the hours a week it is scheduled per machine or crew (two 8-hour shifts, five days, is 80), the number of machines or crews (default: the machines assigned), and the operators per m

title: Shop floor and shift log
text: This page is for the people doing the work. The Shop floor view shows one work center at a time: its machines, the jobs waiting, and who is running what. You start a job, work, then stop it and record what you made. The Shift log is the written handover to the next shift, built partly from those records. Start and stop your own jobs : operators and production supervisors (permission "execute production"). Your user must be linked to an employee record. See the Shop floor menu item : anyone who can execute or manage production. Start a run for someone else : production supervisors (permission "manage production"). Write, hand over and acknowledge a shift log : anyone who can execute or manage work orders or production (technicians, operators, supervisors, managers). Everyone who can view work orders or production can read them. Open the shop floor Open Production → Shop floor . Choose the Work center from the list. Each entry shows its site, code, name and how many operations are waiting. If you are already running a job, your work center is chosen for you; otherwise the first work center with work waiting is chosen. Machines lists the machines at this work center with their current state (running, idle, available, planned downtime, unplanned downtime, out of service) and the qualifications an operator needs. Waiting here lists operations ready to run: order number, operation, work instruction link, part, quantity waiting and due date. "More to come" means the previous operation has not yet passed units on. Running now lists everyone currently running a job, the machine, and how long they have been going. A work instruction link opens the approved version of the instruction in the document viewer. See Document control . Start a job Choose the work center. Check Waiting here for your order and operation. If you are about to set up rather than run, change Record as from Production run to Setup . Setup time is recorded but setup produces no good units. If the work center has more than one machine, choose the machine in the box beside the order. Click Start . The Start button only shows when units are waiting. The system refuses to start the job, and says why, if: your user is not linked to an employee record (a supervisor can record the run for you); you already have a job running (stop it first, even if it is at another work center); the machine is already running another job; the machine is in unplanned downtime or out of service until maintenance returns it to service; you do not hold a qualification the machine requires (see Training and performance ); the machine is an instrument or gauge that is overdue or failed calibration (see Quality ); the operation is finished already, or the order is no longer open. When the job starts the order becomes In progress and the machine's state is set to running. Stop a job and record what you made When you are running a job, a box called Your job appears at the top of the page for that work center. Enter Good : the units that passed. Setup runs have no Good field. Enter Scrap : the units thrown away. If it is above zero, choose a Scrap reason from the list. If some of the good units needed rework first, enter that count in Of the good, reworked . It cannot be more than Good. Add a Note (optional): what happened, adjustments you made. Click Stop and record . You cannot report more units than the operation received. If the numbers don't fit, the message tells you how many units it received and how many are already reported. Check with your supervisor rather than guessing. If you have a job running at a different work center, a yellow notice tells you which order and operation to stop first. After you stop Good units flow to the next operation. When the last operation reports good units, a supervisor receives them into stock from the order page (see Production orders ). If scrap was recorded, quality staff can raise a nonconformance for it from the order's shop-floor record (see Quality ). The shift log Open Production → Shift log . It lists the logs for a site, newest first. Pick the site at the top. Status Meaning Draft Being written. The compiled facts are live and keep updating. Handed over, not yet read The writer has handed over. The facts are now frozen. The row is highlighted until the next shift reads it. Acknowledged Someone on the next shift read it and took over. Their name and time are on the log. The list also shows area, who wrote it, open items (with a red tag for open safety items), machines down, and who read it. Write up your shift At the top of the Shift log page, optionally type an Area . Leave it blank for the whole site. Click Write up this shift . A new log opens, covering the last eight hours. It is named 1st, 2nd or 3rd by the site's local hour (shifts ending 06:00 to 14:00 are "1st", to 22:00 "2nd", otherwise "3rd"). Read the facts the system compiled: machines down, urgent work orders open, what was made and scrapped per work center, orders that are behind, nonconformances, and open SPC signals. You do not have to retype these. Under Safety , write anything the next shift must know: spills, bypassed guards, lockouts left in place. Safety incidents reported this shift are listed under it. Under Open items , pick a category (safety, equipment, quality, production, people, other), write what the next shift should follow up, and click Add . Write how the shift went under Notes and click Save notes . Click Hand over to the next shift . Items still open from the previous log are carried into your new log automatically, marked "carried from". When one is dealt with, type how in How it was resolved and click Resolved . Unresolved items keep carrying forward until someone resolves them. Starting a log when you already have a draft for the same site and area opens that draft rather than a second one. The shift log covers at most 24 hours. Read a handover Open the log marked Handed over, not yet read . Read the safety box, ope

title: Quality
text: The Quality page is where problems with product are recorded and dealt with. Anyone who finds something wrong raises a nonconformance (an "NCR"): a record that something does not meet its requirements. Quality staff then contain it, decide what happens to the material, and, for serious problems, fix the cause with a corrective action (see CAPA and 8D ). The same page holds SPC control charts, FMEA, calibration plans, audits and your own assigned actions. Raise a nonconformance, record SPC measurements : operators, technicians, buyers and most managers (permission "report quality problems"). See everything on the page : quality reviewers, quality managers, plant, maintenance and EHS managers (permission "view quality"). People who can only report see the My actions tab. Contain, disposition, hold lots, close or cancel an NCR; answer SPC signals; set limits; plan calibration and audits; open corrective actions : quality reviewers and quality managers (permission "manage quality"), for their sites. Open Quality & safety → Quality . The tabs are Nonconformances , Corrective actions , FMEA and SPC (only if those features are on for your company), Calibration , Audits and My actions . Raise a nonconformance On the Nonconformances tab click Raise a nonconformance . Choose the Site , where it was found ( Internal , Production , Receiving , Supplier or Customer ), and the severity. Optionally find the part and enter the quantity affected. Describe What is wrong . State facts. Click Raise . The NCR opens. You can add photos and files at the bottom. Severity Use it when Minor A small departure with no effect on safety, fit or customer requirements. Major The product would not meet its requirements or the customer's. Critical A safety, legal or serious customer risk. You can also raise an NCR from a production order that scrapped parts ( Raise NCR in its shop-floor record), from an SPC signal, or from a calibration found out of tolerance. Those NCRs are linked to where they came from. A production run can only have one NCR. What the NCR statuses mean Status Meaning Next Open Raised but not contained. Major and critical ones are highlighted in red. Record containment. Contained Something has been done to stop it spreading: quarantine, sort, hold. Decide the disposition. Dispositioned A decision has been made about the material. Close it, once any needed corrective action is in place. Closed Finished. Held lots are released if the disposition allows. — Cancelled Raised in error or a duplicate, with a reason. — Work an NCR through The NCR page has three numbered sections. A quality manager works down them. Containment. Type what was done to stop it spreading and click Record containment . The NCR becomes Contained. Hold lots, if the part is lot tracked. Under Lots of … tick the lots and click Put the chosen lots on hold . A held lot cannot be issued or shipped. Disposition. Choose Scrap , Rework to drawing , Repair (concession) , Use as is (concession) or Return to supplier (needs a supplier on the NCR). Optionally enter the cost; for scrap, leaving it blank uses quantity times unit cost. Click Record disposition . Corrective action. If the NCR is major or critical it needs one before it can close. Either link an open one from the list or click Open a corrective action . For minor ones it is optional. Click Close nonconformance . Accepting a major or critical NCR "as is" or by repair is a concession . It needs a written justification (who accepted it and why), and it must be recorded by someone other than the person who reported it. Held lots are released when the NCR closes after use as is, rework or repair. Lots that were scrapped or returned stay held until they leave stock. A supplier NCR also has a link to ask that supplier for a corrective action from the supplier's page; the supplier's answer is recorded on the corrective action. To cancel an NCR, type why it is not a nonconformance and click Cancel . SPC control charts Statistical process control (SPC) is a way of watching a measurement over time so you act on a trend before parts go out of tolerance. Each characteristic (for example "bore diameter at op 30") has its own chart. The SPC tab lists the characteristics with their status and capability. Status Meaning Signal open A rule was broken and no one has answered it yet. Investigate. Rule broken, answered A signal happened and has been answered. In control Limits are set and recent points are within them. Initial study Not enough data for firm limits yet; the chart shows trial limits. Not measured No recent measurements. Open the characteristic. The chart shows each point, the centre line, the upper and lower control limits (UCL and LCL) and, for single readings, the tolerance limits. To record a measurement, enter the values under Record a reading (or Record a subgroup of N , with one box per value in the group), with an optional lot and note, and click Record . The message tells you at once whether a rule was broken. If so, quality has been told: stop and check the process. Quality managers answer open signals: click Answer , enter the cause (or "none found") and what was done, optionally raise a nonconformance or exclude the point because of an assignable cause, and click Close the signal . Or click Open a CAPA . Once at least 20 included subgroups exist, a quality manager can click Set limits from all N included subgroups and give a reason. The page shows Cpk and Ppk (how comfortably the process fits within tolerance; 1.33 or more is the usual target). Out-of-tolerance values always alert quality. Which rules raise alarms is set for the whole company and can be changed per characteristic, under Rules . Pass/fail counts (defective parts or defects per unit) use p, np, c and u charts instead. A daily alarm summary appears at the top of the SPC tab. Corrective actions tab This tab lists open corrective actions, with a box to show only yours. Click one to open it. How

title: CAPA and 8D
text: CAPA means corrective and preventive action. A corrective action deals with a problem that has happened: it finds the root cause, fixes it, and later checks that the fix held. A preventive action deals with a problem that has not happened yet but could. An 8D is a corrective action run in an eight-discipline format, which customers often require after a complaint. All three use the same screens. See the CAPA page and list : quality reviewers, quality managers and other staff with "view quality". Open a CAPA, change its owner, record the effectiveness check : quality reviewers and quality managers (permission "manage quality"). Edit a CAPA and add actions : its owner, or a quality manager. For a CAPA that came from a safety incident, a safety manager can also edit it. Do an action assigned to you : the action's owner. The CAPA page Open Quality & safety → CAPA & 8D . A sentence at the top gives the headline. The tiles show open CAPAs (split into corrective and preventive), overdue ones, how many wait for an effectiveness check, the share of fixes that held over the last 12 months, the average days to close, and how many 8Ds are in progress. Tables show open CAPAs by step, by age and by source, and Repeat problems : any part or supplier that needed more than one corrective action this year. Below, the Open list can be filtered to corrective only or preventive only. Overdue ones are marked in red. Open a CAPA A quality manager clicks Open a CAPA . CAPAs also start from other pages: a nonconformance ( Open a corrective action ), a safety incident, an audit finding, an SPC signal, an FMEA row, a change that did not achieve its purpose, and a supplier problem. Those arrive already linked to where they came from. Choose Corrective (a problem that happened) or Preventive (a problem that could happen). Choose the site and the source: internal finding, customer complaint, audit, supplier, SPC alarm, change, FMEA, management review, or risk or trend. Preventive actions can't use customer complaint or supplier as the source. Choose the owner (someone with access to the site), the priority and the due date (the default is 30 days). Write a title and the problem statement: what, where, when, how many. For a corrective action, tick Run as an 8D if the customer asked for one. Click Open corrective action (or preventive action ). The steps and what each needs The CAPA page shows a progress bar with these steps. The owner or a quality manager moves it forward with the button at the bottom. Each step checks its evidence first. Step Meaning To move on Containment Protect the customer while you investigate. Record the containment, or state that none was needed. Root cause Find why it happened. State the root cause and how it was found (5 whys, fishbone, 8D or other). Actions Do the work that removes the cause. Finish or cancel every open action, with at least one done. Effectiveness check Wait, then check that the fix held. Quality records the result (see below). Closed The check showed the fix worked. — Cancelled Dropped. — Open the CAPA and fill Containment and Root cause as you learn them. Click Save when the button appears. Under Actions type the New action , choose an owner and due date, and click Add action . Each owner gets it on My actions (see Quality ). Owners type what was done and click Done . A note of at least three characters is needed. Attach evidence and files at the bottom of the page. Click Move to … at each step. A CAPA from a supplier problem also has a Supplier section where you record the supplier's answer (their root cause and containment can be copied across). It shows whether the answer is waiting, answered, or past due. The effectiveness check When you move to the effectiveness check, a date is set 30 days ahead unless one was already set. The check is done by quality, not by the owner, and not before that date. The owner can lengthen the wait but not shorten it. When the date arrives, a quality manager who is not the owner opens the CAPA. Choose Effective: close it or Not effective: more actions needed . Under Evidence , enter the data, audits or samples that show it (at least ten characters). Click Record check . "Effective" closes the CAPA, and nonconformances waiting on it can then close. "Not effective" sends it back to the Actions step. Running an 8D An 8D is chosen when the CAPA is opened, or by clicking Run as an 8D while it is still at the Containment step. It adds an 8D disciplines checklist that shows what each of the eight still needs. The server checks the same list before each step. Discipline What it needs Needed before you leave D1 Team A champion (someone who can give the team time and resources, other than the owner) and at least one team member besides the leader and champion. The owner is the team leader. Containment D2 Problem description The problem statement and an is / is not table: what it is, where, and at least one thing it is not. Containment D3 Interim containment The containment, and how you know it works. Containment D4 Root causes Why it happened, how it was found, where it should have been caught (escape point), why it was not, and how the causes were confirmed. Root cause D5 Permanent corrective actions At least one action marked "Corrective (D5)". Actions D6 Implemented and validated The corrective actions done, and the effectiveness check. Closed by the check D7 Prevent recurrence Systemic changes recorded (or why none are needed), and every read-across decided. A read-across lists where else the same cause could act; for each, say whether it applies and what was found or done. Actions D8 Team recognized After closure, record what the team achieved. The team is told. After closing For an 8D, each action is marked containment (D3), corrective (D5) or preventive (D7). Click 8D report to open the customer report as a PDF. Preventive actions A preventive action uses the same steps but is described as a potential problem and wh

title: Document control
text: Document control makes sure the people doing a job use the right version of its instructions. Procedures (SOPs), work instructions, test methods, forms, drawings, manuals, customer specifications and standards live in one repository. Each revision is written by one person, approved by another, and takes effect on a stated date. Old revisions are kept but marked as replaced, and every time someone opens a document it is logged. This is the "documented information" an auditor asks for under ISO 9001 clause 7.5. Read approved documents : almost everyone ("view documents"). Restricted documents need the extra "view restricted documents" permission, and a folder or document can be limited to named roles. See drafts : people with "view draft documents", such as technicians, managers and quality staff. Create documents, upload revisions, send for review, link, make folders, run the audit pack : people with "manage documents", for example maintenance managers, quality managers and facilities managers. Approve a revision or make a document obsolete : people with "approve documents" at the site, such as maintenance managers and administrators in the starter roles. Your company may have given the permission to other roles. The repository Open Quality & safety → Document control . A sentence at the top summarises the state. The tiles show controlled documents, external ones (customer specifications and standards), those in review, those waiting for their effective date, and those waiting on you. Use the search box (number, title, issuer's number, or text), and filters for kind, origin (internal or external), folder and status. A row without a revision in force is highlighted. The Next column shows a coming revision or one in review. People who may view reports also see a link to the master list report. Kinds of document Standard operating procedure, work instruction, procedure, method (test or inspection), technical requirement, customer specification, standard, form or template, drawing, manual, troubleshooting guide, repair procedure, service bulletin, training material, photo, video, contract and other. Customer specifications and standards are external : we control our copy and where it applies, but someone else owns the content. All others are internal. If you don't give a number, one is assigned from a prefix per kind (for example SOP-, WI-, TM-). Create a document Click New document . Choose the Kind , optionally a number, the Site (or company-wide) and Folder , and enter the title and a purpose and scope. For an external kind, enter who issued it, their number and revision, and the date you received it. Upload the First version file and give your Our revision label (for example A). Or, for a procedure, work instruction or method, tick Write the steps here in the app instead of uploading a file (see below). Tick Restricted readers only or Safety-critical if they apply, then click Create document . The first version is a draft . Nobody else can use it until it is approved. PDFs, images and text open in the browser; other file types are downloaded. Companies moving from another system can load many files at once with Bring in files from another system (a zip with an index sheet; it is checked first and nothing loads until it is clean). What the statuses mean Status Meaning Draft Uploaded, not yet sent for review. Not approved for use. In review Waiting for reviewers and the approver to sign. Approved, effective on a date Approved, but not yet in force. The previous revision still applies until the date. In force The revision everyone must use. Superseded Replaced by a newer revision. Don't work to it. Obsolete The document is withdrawn, with a reason. Don't use it. Whenever you open a revision that is not the one in force, a red banner says so, with a button to show the revision in force. Revise, review and approve Open the document. Under Control choose New revision : upload the file, give a label, and say What changed and why . The reason is required for every revision after the first. Only one draft can exist at a time. Click Upload as a draft . Choose reviewers if you want them (up to eight; they sign first) and the Approver . The approver must be someone else than the author and must hold approval rights at the site. Set Effective from , or leave it empty to put the revision in force as soon as it is approved. Choose a later date to train people first. It cannot be in the past. Click Send for review . Reviewers and the approver get the request in Home and approvals . Each must add a comment with their decision; the comment is the meaning of their signature. When the approver approves, the revision is released. A released revision's content can never change; corrections need a new revision. Someone with approval rights who isn't the author can also use Approve now (one step) from a draft. The author can never approve their own revision. To pull a revision back, use Withdraw from review with a reason, or Discard the draft . To retire a document, an approver clicks Make obsolete with a reason of at least five characters, once no revision is in review. You can compare any two revisions line by line under Compare revisions : added lines show with + and removed lines with −. Work instructions written in the app For a procedure, work instruction, SOP or method you can write the steps in the app instead of uploading a file. Click Write the steps in the app (or Edit the steps of revision X ). Fill in the purpose, scope, hazards, protective equipment and tools (one per line), then add numbered steps, each with optional caution, a check or measurement with its specification, and photos. Move steps up or down. Click Save as a draft and send it for review like any other revision. Hazards show first when someone reads it. Reading and printing A document opens in the viewer showing the revision in force. A notice reminds you that online copies are controlled and printed copies are not. A print

title: Safety
text: The Safety page is for reporting anything that hurt someone, nearly hurt someone, damaged property or harmed the environment. Reporting a near miss is the cheapest way to fix a hazard. Anyone can report. The safety team then classifies the report, finds the root cause, assigns actions and closes it. Details about injured people are visible only to the safety team. Report something : nearly every role, including operators, technicians, store managers, quality staff and managers (permission "report safety"). You see your own reports under My reports . See all incidents at a site : EHS/safety reviewers, plant and maintenance managers, facilities and district managers and executives (permission "view safety"). They do not see who was injured or the injury details. Classify, investigate, assign actions, open a corrective action, close, and see injury details : EHS/safety reviewers (permission "manage safety"). Report something Open Quality & safety → Safety . If you can only report, the page opens on Report something . Choose the kind: Near miss , First aid , Injury , Illness , Property damage or Environmental . Choose the Site (if you have more than one) and check When . The time can't be in the future. Enter Where (area, line, dock) and pick the equipment if any was involved. Under What happened (facts, not blame) describe it plainly. Optionally write What was done right away . Click Send report . The report opens. You can add photos and files. You do not need to name the injured person. The safety team records who was involved and the details. The notification the safety team receives carries only the kind, place and report number, never private details. Report first, tidy later. If someone is hurt, get help first, then report. Don't wait to know the cause. What the statuses mean Status Meaning What happens next Reported Received, not yet classified. Highlighted in the list. The safety team classifies it. If it's still unclassified a day later, a reminder goes to the safety staff at the site. Investigating Classified; being investigated. The team records the root cause and assigns actions. Actions The root cause is recorded; the fixes are underway. Owners complete the actions, then the safety team closes it. Closed Finished. — Work an incident (safety team) The Incidents tab shows three tiles: reports not yet classified, open reports, and near misses. Tick Only open to hide closed ones. Click a row to open it. Click Classify . Choose the severity ( Low , Medium , High or Serious ) and confirm the kind. For a person involved, choose the employee and enter the injury or illness (nature, body part), whether treatment beyond first aid was given, days away and days restricted, and whether the case is Recordable . Days away or restricted duty make a case recordable; the system refuses "no" in that case. Click Save classification . Click Record root cause . Enter the root cause and any contributing factors, and save. Under Actions , type the New action , pick an owner and due date, and click Add action . Owners find it on My actions , and the owner is told. For a problem that needs a deeper fix, click Open a corrective action . It opens linked to the incident. See CAPA and 8D . When every action is done or cancelled, click Close incident . The system will not let you close an incident until it is classified, an injury or illness has a recordable decision, and a root cause is recorded (the only exception is a low-severity near miss or first-aid case), and no action is still open. Who sees what Everyone who can view safety sees the number, time, kind, place, equipment, severity and status. The person involved, injury description, treatment and days away or restricted are visible only to the safety team. Photos and files can be marked restricted so only the safety team and the person who uploaded them can open them. Reporters see a thank-you note when they open their own report. My actions The My actions tab lists the actions assigned to you across the Quality and Safety areas, with overdue ones marked. Type what was done and click Done . Safety and the shift log Incidents reported during a shift are listed in the safety box of that shift's log, and a safety item left open carries from shift to shift. See Shift log . Common mistakes Not reporting near misses. They are how problems get fixed before someone is hurt. Writing blame instead of facts. Describe what happened. The investigation looks for causes. Putting private details in the description. Leave names and injury details to the safety team, who record them where only they can see. The safety team's access is controlled by role: give "manage safety" to the people who should see injury details. The reminder for unclassified incidents is configurable. Safety can be switched off per company. See Sites and people , Reminders and retention and Features and editions .

title: Changes and notices
text: Management of change (MOC) makes sure a change to equipment, operating limits, materials, software, procedures or staffing is reviewed by the right people before anyone uses it, and that the follow-up work (documents, training, work orders, tests) is done and checked. A change notice (an engineering change notice, or ECN, and similar) is how you tell colleagues, customers and suppliers about a change and keep a record of who has acknowledged. Both are on the Changes page, which also holds temporary SOP changes . See changes and notices : most staff (permission "view changes"), including trainers and managers. Request a change, answer the screening questions on your own request, start a temporary SOP change : operators, technicians, buyers and most managers (permission "request changes"). Act as change coordinator : maintenance managers and plant managers (permission "manage changes"). They link work orders, complete actions on other people's behalf, open the pre-startup review, close changes, raise and issue notices, and approve temporary SOP changes. Review and authorize : the people holding the reviewing roles the change needs (safety and environmental, quality, maintenance and engineering), and finally the plant (operations) manager. Request a change Open Quality & safety → Changes and click Request a change . Choose the Facility and the Type of change : equipment, process, procedure, material, controls software, organizational, facility or other. Write a Title , What will change? and Why? (at least ten characters each for the last two). Under Planning the change , say whether it is Planned (nothing changes until approved), Emergency (already made to protect people, product or equipment) or Unintended (found after it happened). Describe the consequences, what it changes in the quality system (processes, documents, records), the resources it needs, and who is responsible. These four are required before review. Say whether customers are unaffected, must be told, or must approve it first. If they are affected, name them and what they must be told or approve. Optionally set a target date, tick Temporary change with a removal date (up to 180 days), and tick the affected equipment. Click Save draft . On the change page you can attach the presentation behind the justification (a PowerPoint or PDF, or an https link) while it is a draft. Every version of an uploaded deck is kept. Screening and review On the draft, answer all nine Screening questions Yes or No. They ask whether the change affects safety systems, introduces a new chemical or material, changes operating limits, affects controls software, product quality, the environment, procedures, training or staffing. Click Submit for review . The answers decide, by fixed rules (shown on the page as "Screened with"), the risk level (low, medium, high), which reviews are needed (safety and environmental, quality, maintenance and engineering), and whether a pre-startup safety review is required (it is for high risk, and for changes to safety systems or new chemicals). The system also generates the action plan: revise the affected documents, train people, link the work order that implements the change, brief the affected shifts, tell or get approval from customers, a hazard review for high risk, a function test for safety devices, a consequence review for emergency or unintended changes, and a restore action for temporary changes. Reviewers sign in order: first the review roles, then the plant manager authorizes. Each must record what was checked and any conditions. Nobody approves their own request. If a change is revised after approval, its approvals are voided and it must be approved again. If a change is rejected A reviewer who rejects must give a reason, and the change returns to its author for rework. The change page shows a red notice with who rejected it, in which review, when, and the reason. Open the rejected change. The requester, the owner or a change coordinator sees Rework the change . Edit the description, reason, planning answers, customers and target date to answer the reviewer, and click Save changes . You can also attach a better presentation (the justification deck can be replaced while the change is rejected). Saving returns the change to Draft as the next revision. Answer the screening questions again and click Resubmit for review . If nothing needs to change in the fields (for example you only attached the missing deck), you can resubmit straight away from the rejected state. Resubmitting starts a fresh approval round at the next revision number: all reviewers sign again, including those who had already approved, and the action plan generated from the screening is rebuilt (open generated actions are replaced, ones you added yourself stay). The earlier round is not erased: under Sign-offs every round is listed ( Change authorization, round 1 , round 2 …) with its revision, each reviewer's decision and comment, and the History shows Reworked and Resubmitted . What the stages mean Stage Meaning What happens next Draft Being written (or being reworked after a rejection). Screening is not yet answered. Edit if needed, answer screening and submit. Review Waiting for the reviewers and the plant manager to sign. Approved, or rejected. Implement (approved) Authorized. The action plan is carried out. Complete all startup actions, then open the pre-startup review, or put into service. Pre-startup review A checklist of seven questions must be Yes or N/A. Safety and operations sign the startup. In service The change is live. Complete the remaining actions and close it. Closed Finished, with its verified outcome. — Rejected / Cancelled Not authorized (the reason is shown), or dropped with a reason. A rejected change can be reworked and resubmitted (see above). A cancelled one cannot; raise a new request if still needed. An in-service change can't be cancelled; reverse it with a new change. Do the action plan Open the ap

title: Temporary SOP changes
text: Sometimes a procedure has to be different for a while: a part is out of stock so you use a substitute, a machine is down so you use a workaround, a customer allows a deviation. A temporary SOP change records exactly what is different, why, and until when, without rewriting the procedure. While it is in force, everyone who opens that procedure sees a banner with the change and its end date. When the date arrives, the change cannot quietly carry on: it must be reverted, extended or made permanent. Start a temporary change and manage your own : anyone who can request changes, such as operators, technicians, buyers and managers. The person who created it, or its owner, can submit, extend, revert, cancel or make it permanent. Approve, and manage anyone's : change coordinators (maintenance managers and plant managers; permission "manage changes"). Nobody can approve their own change. See them : anyone who can view changes. Where to find it Open Quality & safety → Changes and click the Temporary SOP changes tab. The tiles show how many are in force, how many end within 14 days, and how many are past their end date. Tick Only changes in force or waiting to start to hide finished ones. The Time left column is coloured: Colour Time left Meaning Green More than 14 days No action needed yet. Amber 4 to 14 days Start deciding what happens at the end. Red 3 days or fewer Decide now. Red, "days over" The end date has passed Expired. The procedure still carries the change. Act at once. Start a temporary change Click New temporary change . Choose the Site and the Procedure . The list shows controlled SOPs, work instructions, procedures, methods, repair procedures, manuals and troubleshooting guides that have an approved revision. Set Starts (today by default) and Ends . The end cannot be before the start or in the past. Write a short Title , then What is different while it is in force (at least ten characters) and Why it is needed . Click Save draft . On the change page, under Next step , choose an Approver (a change coordinator at the site, other than you) and click Submit for approval . The whole period, from start to end, can't be longer than the company's ceiling (90 days unless your administrator changed it). For anything longer, change the procedure itself. What the statuses mean Status Meaning What happens next Draft Being written. Submit it for approval, or cancel. Waiting for approval The approver has been asked. On approval it starts (see below). Not approved sends it back to you. Not approved The approver refused it. You are told. Revise and submit again, or cancel. Approved, not started Approved, but the start date is still ahead. It goes into force on the start date. In force Live. The banner is shown on the procedure. It runs to its end date unless reverted, extended or made permanent. Expired: needs a decision The end date passed and nobody has resolved it. The banner stays up, marked as past its end date. Revert, extend or make permanent. Becoming permanent A normal change has been opened to put the wording into the procedure. The banner and timer keep running until that change is approved. Reverted The procedure is back to its approved form. Finished. Made permanent The change for it was approved. Finished. Cancelled Dropped before it began. Finished. What readers see While a change is in force (or expired and unresolved), a banner appears at the top of the procedure, including a work instruction written in the app. It reads Temporary change in force with the change number, what is different, the end date and the days left. Past the end date it reads Temporary change past its end date . The banner links to the details. Treat it as part of the procedure. Expiry timers and alerts A daily check runs for every change that is in force. The change's owner is alerted at 14, 7, 3, 1 and 0 days before the end date. The approver is also alerted at 3, 1 and 0 days. Each alert is sent once. If the end date passes and the change is not resolved: the status changes to Expired: needs a decision ; the owner is alerted every day ; from the seventh day, change coordinators at the site are alerted as well (escalation), every day, until it is resolved. There is also a weekly reminder for temporary changes ending soon, which your administrator can switch off or adjust. It is separate from the daily alerts above. Extend, revert or make permanent When the end is near, or after it has passed, you have three ways to resolve the change. Use the Next step card on the change page. Extend Under Extend , choose a New end date later than the current one. Give a Reason (at least five characters) and choose an approver. Click Request extension . Each extension needs its own reason and fresh approval. One extension can add at most the company's ceiling in days, counted from the later of the current end date or today. Only one request can wait at a time. If the approver refuses, you are told to revert or make it permanent. A change extended twice or more shows a warning: if it is still needed, make it permanent. Revert Put the procedure back to its normal form and tell the people who used the change. Type a note confirming that (at least five characters). Click Revert: procedure is back to normal . The banner disappears. Make permanent Click Make it permanent (opens a change) . A normal change of the type "procedure" is created, linked to the procedure, with the temporary wording as its description. Take it through the usual steps in Changes and notices , and revise the document through Document control . The banner and the timer keep running until that change is approved. Then the temporary change is marked Made permanent . If the change is rejected or cancelled, the temporary change returns to its previous state. Cancel A draft, a change waiting for approval, or a change that was not approved can be cancelled with a reason. Once a change has been approved, use Revert instead. title: Business continuity
text: A continuity plan answers one question for one critical process: if this stops, how do we get it running again, how fast, and who do we call? It lists what the process depends on (a machine, a supplier, a skill, a person), what could go wrong, the recovery steps for each case, and who owns them. The plan is then tested with exercises. The system also checks the plan against live records and shows the gaps, so a plan that was true last year does not quietly go stale. See plans : plant, maintenance and facilities managers, EHS and quality staff, executives and others with "view continuity". A plan's owner and alternate can always see it. Create a plan, edit it, schedule exercises, record results, add actions, review and revise : the plan's owner or alternate, and anyone with "manage continuity" (plant managers and EHS/safety reviewers). Approve the plan : the plant (operations) manager. The plan list Open Quality & safety → Continuity . The tiles show how many plans exist, how many are approved, how many have shown their recovery time in a timed exercise, and how many have high gaps. Each row shows the process, its criticality (critical, high, medium), the RTO, the recovery time actually shown, the last exercise, when the review is due, and gaps and open actions. Plans with high gaps are highlighted. RTO (recovery time objective) How long the process can be down before the damage is unacceptable.
